title.rendered: Best Fashion Designers: 15 Designers to Know — Global Icons and Indian Greats

content.rendered:
Fashion's biggest names divide into two kinds of greatness. Some designers invented the clothes the rest of the world still wears, from the little black dress to the unstructured jacket. Others built houses that outlived them, passing through new creative directors while keeping a recognisable code.

This guide profiles 15 designers to know in 2026: nine global figures whose work set the template for modern luxury, and six Indian designers who built an industry around craft, couture and the wedding wardrobe. Every entry reflects the position as of November 2026, a moment when several great houses are changing hands, changing designers, or both.

Quick Answer: The 15 Designers at a Glance

  • Coco Chanel — freed women from corsets and gave fashion the little black dress, the tweed suit and Chanel No. 5.
  • Christian Dior — founded his house in 1946 and reset post-war fashion with the 1947 New Look.
  • Yves Saint Laurent — put women in tuxedos with Le Smoking and took couture to the high street with ready-to-wear.
  • Giorgio Armani — softened the suit into modern tailoring and built an independent empire; he died in September 2025.
  • Ralph Lauren — turned an idealised American lifestyle into a global label; first designer to receive the US Presidential Medal of Freedom.
  • Karl Lagerfeld — ran Chanel for 36 years and Fendi for over five decades, the defining creative director of his era.
  • Donatella Versace — led Versace for nearly 28 years after her brother Gianni's death, stepping down as creative chief in 2025.
  • Alexander McQueen — fused Savile Row tailoring with dark, theatrical spectacle.
  • Vivienne Westwood — dressed punk, then turned the runway into a platform for climate protest.
  • Ritu Kumar — India's pioneering designer label, built on reviving handloom textiles and traditional embroidery.
  • Rohit Bal — the showman of Indian couture, famed for lotus motifs and velvet grandeur; he died in November 2024.
  • Tarun Tahiliani — created the 'India Modern' formula of draped, structured couture, now 30 years into his label.
  • Sabyasachi Mukherjee — made heritage bridal maximalism a global business, marking 25 years of his label in 2025.
  • Manish Malhotra — Bollywood's defining costume designer turned couturier, now a fixture on global red carpets.
  • Masaba Gupta — the youngest name here, who turned bold statement prints into a fashion and beauty business.

The 15 Designers in Summary

The Global Icons

1. Coco Chanel

Gabrielle 'Coco' Chanel (1883–1971) began with a Paris millinery shop in 1910 and spent six decades dismantling the corseted silhouette. She worked in jersey when it was considered underwear fabric, cut suits from tweed, and treated comfort as a luxury. The house she founded remains privately owned and is still the benchmark for a brand built on one woman's codes.

Those codes now pass to a fourth artistic director. Matthieu Blazy, appointed in December 2024 after his success at Bottega Veneta, showed his first Chanel collection in Paris in October 2025 and his first haute couture collection in January 2026, reworking tweed, tailoring and the house's symbols to strong reviews.

  • Label: Chanel, Paris — founded as a millinery shop in 1910
  • Signature: the little black dress (1926), the collarless tweed suit, costume jewellery worn with couture
  • Enduring product: Chanel No. 5, launched in 1921 and still a global bestseller
  • Today: artistic director Matthieu Blazy, in post since 2025

2. Christian Dior

Christian Dior (1905–1957) opened his Paris house in 1946 and, in February 1947, presented the collection a fashion editor dubbed the 'New Look': nipped waists, padded hips and skirts using yards of fabric. After wartime austerity it was a sensation, and it restored Paris as fashion's capital. Dior died just a decade later, but the house became the template for the designer-led luxury group.

In June 2025 the house unified its creative direction for the first time since Dior himself. Jonathan Anderson, after eleven years transforming Loewe, now oversees womenswear, menswear and haute couture together. His menswear debuted in June 2025 and his womenswear that October, shrinking the famous Bar jacket and mixing it with cargo shorts and period dress.

  • Label: Dior, Paris — founded 1946, owned by LVMH
  • Signature: the Bar jacket and the hourglass New Look silhouette
  • Turning point: the February 1947 collection that revived Paris couture
  • Today: creative director Jonathan Anderson across women's, men's and couture since 2025

3. Yves Saint Laurent

Yves Saint Laurent (1936–2008) was hired by Christian Dior as a teenager and succeeded him at just 21. In 1961 he founded his own house with Pierre Bergé. His genius was translation: art into prints, menswear into womenswear, and couture into ready-to-wear with his Rive Gauche line, which changed how designer clothes were sold.

The house he left behind has just closed a chapter. Anthony Vaccarello, creative director since 2016, presented a golden final collection in Paris in September 2026, and Kering confirmed his departure that October after a decade in which the brand's sales more than trebled at their peak. A successor had yet to be announced as this guide was updated.

  • Label: Saint Laurent, Paris — founded 1961, owned by Kering
  • Signature: Le Smoking tuxedo for women (1966), safari jackets, sheer blouses
  • Turning point: Rive Gauche (1966), the first luxury ready-to-wear line by a couturier
  • Today: between creative directors, following Anthony Vaccarello's exit in October 2026

4. Giorgio Armani

Giorgio Armani (1934–2025) co-founded his company in Milan in 1975 with Sergio Galeotti and built it into the great independent house of Italian fashion. His idea was subtraction: remove the padding and stiffness from tailoring and let the cloth move. The soft jacket became the uniform of a new professional class, on screen in American Gigolo and in boardrooms everywhere.

Armani died on 4 September 2025, aged 91, having planned his succession in unusual detail. His will directs his heirs to sell an initial 15 per cent stake, naming LVMH, L'Oréal and EssilorLuxottica as preferred partners, while the Giorgio Armani Foundation keeps at least 30 per cent. Long-serving executive Giuseppe Marsocci became chief executive in October 2025, and collections continue under the house's own studio, led on menswear by the founder's partner Leo Dell'Orco.

  • Label: Giorgio Armani, Milan — founded 1975, still privately held
  • Signature: deconstructed tailoring in muted 'greige' tones
  • Turning point: dressing Richard Gere in American Gigolo (1980)
  • Today: founder-led era ended in 2025; a staged stake sale is under way under his will

5. Ralph Lauren

Ralph Lauren (born 1939) started in 1967 selling wide neckties, then built Polo Ralph Lauren into the complete wardrobe of an imagined America: Ivy League blazers, western shirts, polo shirts with the embroidered player. He sold a lifestyle before the industry had the word for it, extending the same world into homeware, restaurants and Olympic team uniforms.

In January 2025 he became the first fashion designer to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour in the United States, presented at the White House. He remains executive chairman and chief creative officer of the company that bears his name, nearly six decades after founding it.

  • Label: Ralph Lauren, New York — founded 1967
  • Signature: preppy tailoring, the polo shirt, Americana styling
  • Honour: Presidential Medal of Freedom, January 2025 — a first for a fashion designer
  • Today: still executive chairman and chief creative officer

6. Karl Lagerfeld

Karl Lagerfeld (1933–2019) was the industry's great interpreter. At Fendi from 1965 and at Chanel from 1983, he proved a creative director could revive a dormant house by remixing its founder's codes — in Chanel's case, the tweed, the camellia, the interlocked Cs and the little black jacket — season after season, without repeating himself. His own label, photography and book publishing ran in parallel.

Lagerfeld's workload became the profession's benchmark: multiple collections a year across several houses, staged as spectacles in the Grand Palais. The houses he defined have since moved on — Chanel under Matthieu Blazy is this list's clearest example — but the job description he wrote, custodian and provocateur at once, is the one his successors still follow.

  • Labels: Chanel (1983–2019), Fendi (1965–2019), Karl Lagerfeld
  • Base: Paris
  • Signature: reinvention of heritage codes, spectacle runway shows
  • Legacy: the modern creative-director model — one designer, several houses

7. Donatella Versace

Donatella Versace (born 1955) was her brother Gianni's closest collaborator and muse. When he was murdered in 1997, she took over creative direction of Versace within months and held it for nearly 28 years, keeping the house's baroque prints, gold Medusa hardware and unapologetic glamour alive through fashion's minimalist decades — and dressing the celebrities who kept it famous.

Her tenure ended in March 2025, when she stepped down as chief creative officer to become chief brand ambassador. Versace itself changed owners the same year, with Prada Group completing its purchase from Capri Holdings in December 2025. After a single season under Dario Vitale, Pieter Mulier took over as chief creative officer in July 2026. Donatella, meanwhile, announced a joint venture with Revolve in September 2026 to build a new fashion and beauty label of her own.

  • Label: Versace, Milan — creative director 1997–2025, now chief brand ambassador
  • Signature: baroque prints, safety-pin and jungle dresses, Medusa gold
  • Turning point: holding the house together after Gianni Versace's death in 1997
  • Today: Versace is owned by Prada Group; Donatella is building a new label with Revolve

8. Alexander McQueen

Lee Alexander McQueen (1969–2010) learned his craft as a Savile Row apprentice, and the cutting never left his work. His London shows of the 1990s — the bumster trouser, the Highland Rape and Voss collections — were part tailoring masterclass, part theatre of cruelty and beauty. He ran Givenchy in Paris from 1996 to 2001, then built his own house within the Gucci Group, now Kering.

McQueen's deputy Sarah Burton carried the house for thirteen years after his death in 2010. Seán McGirr, appointed in December 2023, brought a rawer, youth-driven energy across five seasons; Kering announced his departure in October 2026, and the house is again in transition. The founder's combination of precision and provocation remains the standard every successor is measured against.

  • Label: Alexander McQueen, London — founded 1992, owned by Kering
  • Signature: razor-sharp tailoring, skull motifs, dark romantic spectacle
  • Turning point: the Voss show (2000) and Plato's Atlantis (2010), his final collection
  • Today: between creative directors after Seán McGirr's exit in October 2026

9. Vivienne Westwood

Vivienne Westwood (1941–2022) started selling clothes from a King's Road shop in 1971 with Malcolm McLaren, and dressed the punk movement as it happened: torn T-shirts, bondage straps, safety pins as jewellery. Her first runway collection, Pirates, followed in 1981. She spent the next four decades raiding British history — tartan, tweed, the corset, the crinoline — and bending it out of shape.

Westwood died in December 2022, and the house continues under her husband Andreas Kronthaler, its creative director. His collections keep her codes of corsetry and chaotic tailoring, and the brand took her message to India in April 2025 with a Mumbai show at the Gateway of India built partly on handwoven khadi and chanderi silks.

  • Label: Vivienne Westwood, London — shop opened 1971, first collection 1981
  • Signature: punk styling, tartan and Harris Tweed, the revived corset
  • Second act: climate and anti-consumption activism on the runway
  • Today: creative director Andreas Kronthaler, her widower and long-time collaborator

The Indian Greats

10. Ritu Kumar

Ritu Kumar (born 1944) is the founder figure of Indian designer fashion. Starting in 1969 with hand-block printers in Kolkata, she built India's first major designer label on a simple argument: the country's handloom textiles and embroideries — zardozi, chikankari, kalamkari — deserved couture status. When few took craft seriously as fashion, she documented and revived dying techniques village by village.

The label is now helmed by her son Amrish Kumar, with the founder still its guiding presence. At Hyundai India Couture Week in July 2025 she presented Threads of Time: Reimagined, a five-decade retrospective of her prints and bridal craft reworked in sheer layers, corsetry and crystal — a reminder that the revival she started is now the mainstream of Indian occasionwear.

  • Label: Ritu Kumar, New Delhi — began 1969; now led by Amrish Kumar
  • Signature: hand-block prints, zardozi and handloom textiles
  • Honour: Padma Shri, 2013, for her contribution to fashion and textiles
  • Today: showing couture at India Couture Week 2025, five decades on

11. Rohit Bal

Rohit Bal (1961–2024), born in Srinagar and trained at St Stephen's College and NIFT Delhi, launched his label in 1986 and became Indian couture's great showman. His clothes were maximal and meticulous at once: lotus and peacock motifs, cascades of embroidery, velvet bandhgalas and ivory anarkalis, presented in shows staged like theatre. He was a founding member of the Fashion Design Council of India.

Bal's ending was as public as his career. Weeks after a serious cardiac illness, he returned to present his final collection, Kaaynaat: A Bloom in the Universe, as the Lakmé Fashion Week x FDCI finale in October 2024, dancing on the ramp at his bow. He died on 1 November 2024, aged 63. His label continues under designer Fraze Tasnim, keeping the house's motifs in production.

  • Label: Rohit Bal, New Delhi — launched 1986
  • Signature: lotus motifs, velvet, ivory and gold couture
  • Final show: Kaaynaat, Lakmé Fashion Week finale, October 2024
  • Today: the house continues under Fraze Tasnim after Bal's death in November 2024

12. Tarun Tahiliani

Tarun Tahiliani (born 1961) founded his label in 1995 and gave Indian couture its most durable formula: 'India Modern'. His insight was construction. By building Western tailoring and corsetry inside Indian garments — the structured drape, the weightless lehenga, the concept sari — he made festive clothes that moved like ready-to-wear and photographed like couture.

The label turned 30 in 2025, marked by the Quintessence couture collection at India Couture Week and an anniversary show in Hyderabad. Tahiliani is now scaling as well as designing: Tasva, his menswear label with Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail, has grown to dozens of stores, his prêt label OTT is expanding, a high jewellery line, TT Tijori, has launched, and a first Dubai store is planned.

  • Label: Tarun Tahiliani, New Delhi — founded 1995
  • Signature: 'India Modern' — draped, structured, feather-light couture
  • Business: Tasva menswear and OTT prêt, backed by Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail
  • Today: 30 years in, expanding retail in India and planning Dubai

13. Sabyasachi Mukherjee

Sabyasachi Mukherjee (born 1974) launched his label from Kolkata in 1999 with a conviction the market initially resisted: that Indian brides would pay couture prices for heritage — for Banarasi weaves, antique embroidery techniques and jewellery with old-world weight. He was right. The 'Sabyasachi bride' became a category of her own, and his red bridal lehengas a default reference for celebrity weddings.

In January 2025 he marked 25 years of the label with one of Indian fashion's largest shows, at Mumbai's Jio World Centre: more than 150 looks on a set recreating old Kolkata, opened by Deepika Padukone and closed by Christy Turlington. With Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail holding a majority stake since 2021, his stated focus now is global expansion, led by jewellery and accessories.

  • Label: Sabyasachi, Kolkata — founded 1999
  • Signature: heritage bridal maximalism, antique textiles, statement jewellery
  • Milestone: 25th anniversary show, Mumbai, January 2025 — over 150 looks
  • Today: expanding internationally, with jewellery and accessories the growth lines

14. Manish Malhotra

Manish Malhotra (born 1966) shaped how India imagines glamour, first through cinema. From 1990 he designed costumes for hundreds of Hindi films, setting the look of Bollywood's biggest stars, then launched his label in 2005. His couture — sequins, feathers, sculpted drapes — translates screen glamour into wedding and red-carpet dressing, and Reliance Brands took a 40 per cent stake in 2021.

His 2025 was a global lap of honour, marking 35 years in costume design and 20 years of the label. He was the first Indian designer invited to the Golden Globes, made his Met Gala debut in May 2025 both as attendee and as designer for Coco Jones and Natasha Poonawalla, and closed Dubai Fashion Week with his World Collection. He returned to the Met Gala in 2026.

  • Label: Manish Malhotra, Mumbai — label launched 2005, costume design since 1990
  • Signature: sequinned couture, Bollywood glamour, high jewellery
  • Milestone: Met Gala debut in 2025, as designer and attendee
  • Today: a fixture at Dubai Fashion Week and on global red carpets

15. Masaba Gupta

Masaba Gupta (born 1989), daughter of actor Neena Gupta and cricketer Vivian Richards, launched House of Masaba in 2009 at nineteen. Where Indian occasionwear was heavy and formal, she offered print and wit: palm trees, cows, cameras and lipsticks blown up across kurtas, saris and dresses in hot pink and black. The motifs became logos in all but name, recognisable across a room.

She has since built beyond the label. LoveChild by Masaba, her beauty brand, launched in 2022 and now collaborates well outside cosmetics — its Trousseau luggage collection with American Tourister arrived in November 2025. In 2026 she presented Chardi Kala, House of Masaba's first full bridal collection, extending her print language into the wedding market her peers dominate.

  • Label: House of Masaba, Mumbai — founded 2009
  • Signature: oversized statement prints, hot pink, playful saris
  • Beyond fashion: LoveChild by Masaba beauty brand, launched 2022
  • Today: first bridal collection, Chardi Kala, presented in 2026

Indian Fashion on the Global Stage

The two halves of this list increasingly share a wardrobe. Global houses come to India for craft and customers; Indian designers take Indian clothing to the world's red carpets. The traffic now runs in both directions, and it is changing what both sides make.

  • Craft as currency: Vivienne Westwood showed in Mumbai in 2025 using khadi and chanderi; Dior and Chanel rely on Indian embroidery ateliers for couture embellishment.
  • Indian designers, global stages: Manish Malhotra dressed guests at the Met Gala in 2025 and 2026; Sabyasachi's jewellery is worn on international red carpets.
  • Corporate scale: Reliance Brands and Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail now back several Indian labels, funding the store networks couture alone never could.
  • The wedding economy: bridal couture remains Indian fashion's engine, but prêt labels such as OTT and Tasva show the same houses chasing everyday wardrobes.
  • Succession everywhere: 2025–26 brought new creative directors or transitions at Chanel, Dior, Versace, Saint Laurent and McQueen — and at the Armani and Rohit Bal houses, the harder test of continuing without a founder.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is considered the greatest fashion designer of all time?

There is no single answer, but Coco Chanel and Christian Dior are the most common choices. Chanel changed how women dressed every day; Dior rebuilt an industry with one collection in 1947. Yves Saint Laurent, who worked for Dior before founding his own house, usually completes the top three.

Which designers on this list are still working today?

Ralph Lauren still leads his company, and Donatella Versace remains Versace's chief brand ambassador while building a new label. In India, Ritu Kumar, Tarun Tahiliani, Sabyasachi Mukherjee, Manish Malhotra and Masaba Gupta all actively run their labels. The founders of Chanel, Dior, Saint Laurent, Armani, Lagerfeld, McQueen, Westwood and Rohit Bal have all died, and their houses continue under new leadership.

Who designs Chanel and Dior now?

Matthieu Blazy has been Chanel's artistic director since 2025, only the fourth person to hold the role. At Dior, Jonathan Anderson took over women's, men's and haute couture collections in 2025, the first single creative director across the whole house since Christian Dior himself.

Who is India's most famous fashion designer?

By global reach, Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Manish Malhotra lead: Sabyasachi through bridal couture and jewellery, Malhotra through Bollywood and, since 2025, the Met Gala and Dubai Fashion Week. Ritu Kumar holds the distinction of having started it all, founding India's first major designer label in 1969.

What happened to the house of Armani after Giorgio Armani's death?

Armani died in September 2025, leaving a detailed will. It directs his heirs to sell a first 15 per cent stake to a major luxury partner, with LVMH, L'Oréal and EssilorLuxottica named as preferred buyers, while his foundation retains at least 30 per cent. The group is run by chief executive Giuseppe Marsocci, and collections continue from the house studio.

Why are so many fashion houses changing designers at once?

A luxury slowdown after 2023 pushed owners to refresh their biggest brands. Between 2025 and 2026, Chanel, Dior, Versace, Saint Laurent and Alexander McQueen all changed creative leadership, alongside the succession at Armani. Houses now treat the creative director as a renewable appointment rather than a job for life — the opposite of the founder era most of this list represents.

excerpt.rendered: From Coco Chanel, Christian Dior and Yves Saint Laurent to Ritu Kumar, Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Masaba Gupta — 15 fashion designers to know, each with a verified photograph, the house or label they built, and what they are known for. An editorial selection of global icons and Indian greats.

title.rendered: Top 8 Joysticks for PC in India (2026)

content.rendered:
Search any shopping site for "joystick" and you get two different products mixed together. Most results are gamepads — the twin-stick, two-handed controllers that most PC players actually mean. The rest are flight sticks: a single upright stick, often paired with a separate throttle, made for flight simulators. This guide deals with both honestly: eight gamepads you can order in India today, plus straightforward guidance on flight sticks, a category where Indian availability is patchy at best.

All eight gamepads were re-checked against Amazon India in November 2026. Each review carries the product's real Amazon photo and a button through to its listing, because that listing is the only place with a trustworthy price: Amazon.in figures change with every sale and stock movement, so this guide prints none. What a listing cannot tell you is how the pads differ — connection, stick technology, battery, compatibility — and that comparison is the point of the pages below.

The shortlist pairs the two console-standard controllers from Microsoft and Sony with an officially licensed wired pad from PowerA, and five Indian-market favourites — from Cosmic Byte, EvoFox and Redgear — that add magnetic Hall Effect sticks, tri-mode wireless and back buttons at lower budgets. Football, racing, action RPGs, flight sims: one of the eight will fit.

Quick Answer

In a hurry? Start here:

  • Best for most PC gamers: Xbox Wireless Controller — the layout and connection standard Windows games are built around.
  • Best for haptics and adaptive triggers: Sony DualSense — a more tactile pad, with its special features working in supported PC games.
  • Best wired pad with pro features: PowerA Advantage Plus — Hall Effect sticks, two back buttons and adjustable stick height, officially licensed for Xbox.
  • Best value tri-mode all-rounder: Cosmic Byte Ares Pro — 2.4GHz, Bluetooth and wired in one pad, Hall Effect sticks and triggers included.
  • Best for multi-device gaming: EvoFox Elite X2 Pro — tri-mode connection, HallSense sticks and triggers, and an app for remapping.
  • Best budget tri-mode: EvoFox One S V2 — three connection modes and magnetic HallSense sticks at the low end of the range.
  • Best budget wireless: Redgear Pro Wireless — a simple 2.4GHz dongle pad made for Windows PCs.
  • Best budget wired: Redgear Pro Wired — the same idea with a cable, so there is no battery to charge.

Joystick, Gamepad or Flight Stick — What Do the Words Mean?

The words are used loosely online, but the hardware falls into three distinct kinds:

  • Gamepad: a two-handed controller with two thumbsticks, a D-pad, face buttons and triggers. This is the default controller for modern PC gaming, and all eight products reviewed below are gamepads.
  • Joystick: strictly, a single stick that you grip and tilt. The word survives in everyday speech — many people say "joystick" when they mean a gamepad — and in arcade fight sticks, but as a product category it now mostly means flight hardware.
  • Flight stick / HOTAS: an upright stick, often sold with a separate throttle unit (HOTAS means "hands on throttle and stick"), built for flight and space simulators. See the flight stick section near the end of this guide.

If you play a mix of games, buy a gamepad. If you mainly fly, read the product reviews for general control advice, then go to the flight stick section before spending anything.

How to Choose the Right Controller for Your PC

  • Connection: wired is simplest and never needs charging. A 2.4GHz dongle gives low-latency wireless on a PC. Bluetooth is the most flexible option for phones and tablets, but usually the slowest of the three.
  • XInput support: Windows games are built around the Xbox XInput standard, so a pad that speaks XInput works in almost everything with no set-up. Several pads below can also switch to the older DirectInput standard for legacy games.
  • Stick technology: conventional sticks read position with contact-based sensors that can wear and start to drift. Hall Effect sticks read position magnetically, with no contact surface to wear away.
  • Back buttons and remapping: extra rear buttons let you jump or reload without lifting your thumbs off the sticks. App support varies by brand — Xbox Accessories for Microsoft, Gamer HQ for PowerA, KeyLinker for EvoFox.
  • Battery: some pads run on AA batteries, others on built-in rechargeable cells. Rated running times assume light use, so treat them as a guide rather than a promise.
  • Compatibility beyond PC: if the same pad should also serve a console, a phone or a TV, confirm the maker lists that device for that exact model before you buy.

Quick Comparison

The Best Joysticks and Controllers for PC, Reviewed

1. Xbox Wireless Controller (Carbon Black) — Best for Most PC Gamers

Check price on Amazon

Buy one controller for a Windows PC and never think about controllers again, and it should be this one. Windows games are designed first for the Xbox pad and its XInput protocol, so games pick this controller up the moment it connects — nothing to configure, nothing extra to install. The present design pairs a hybrid D-pad, equally at home in menus and fighting games, with grip texture across the triggers, bumpers and rear casing, and adds a Share button for capturing clips and screenshots.

It connects three ways: Xbox Wireless to a console, Bluetooth to a PC, phone or tablet, and USB-C for wired play. Microsoft rates battery usage at up to 40 hours from the AA batteries it runs on, and a rechargeable battery pack is sold separately. Buttons can be remapped in the Xbox Accessories app. The sticks are conventional rather than Hall Effect, and there are no back buttons — but for plug-and-play reliability across PC and Xbox, nothing else on this list is as safe a buy.

Key facts:

  • Connectivity: Xbox Wireless and Bluetooth, plus USB-C for wired play
  • Hybrid D-pad; textured grip on triggers, bumpers and back case
  • Share button for screenshots and clips; 3.5mm stereo headset jack
  • Runs on AA batteries; Microsoft rates battery usage at up to 40 hours
  • Button remapping available in the Xbox Accessories app
  • Works with Windows 10/11, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Android and iOS

2. Sony DualSense Wireless Controller (White) — Best for Haptics and Adaptive Triggers

Check price on Amazon

Sony's DualSense is the controller for players who want to feel their games. Its haptic feedback uses dual actuators instead of ordinary rumble motors, and its adaptive triggers can change resistance under your fingers — drawing a bow, or braking into a corner. Both features need support from the game itself, and on PC the full haptics need a USB connection, but a growing list of PC releases supports them, and Steam's controller layer makes the pad work well even in games that do not.

It pairs over Bluetooth or USB-C with Windows, Mac, Android, iOS and, of course, a PS5 — and since a September 2025 system update it can stay paired with up to four devices and switch between them from the controller. The built-in rechargeable battery is a 1,560 mAh cell; Sony does not publish a rated running time. You also get a touch pad, a six-axis motion sensor, a built-in microphone with its own mute button and a headset jack. Note that it does not work natively with a PS4.

Key facts:

  • Connectivity: Bluetooth and USB-C wired
  • Haptic feedback and adaptive triggers, where the game supports them
  • Built-in rechargeable 1,560 mAh battery, charged over USB-C
  • Create button, touch pad, motion sensor and built-in microphone with mute button
  • 3.5mm headset jack (on PC, the jack needs the wired connection)
  • Works with Windows 10/11, Mac, Android, iOS and PS5; multi-device pairing since September 2025

3. PowerA Advantage Plus Wired Controller (Night Blossom) — Best Wired Pad with Pro Features

Check price on Amazon

The Advantage Plus is a wired controller with features competitive players usually pay much more for. Its thumbsticks use Hall Effect magnetic sensors, so there is no contact surface inside them to wear into drift, and PowerA's Quick-Twist design lets you set each stick to one of three heights — standard, medium or tall — mid-game, with no parts to swap. This Night Blossom version is a floral design launched in May 2025 on the same hardware.

Two Advanced Gaming Buttons on the back can be mapped on the fly, the triggers carry their own rumble motors — PowerA calls them Impulse Triggers — and dual rumble motors sit in the grips. The free PowerA Gamer HQ app adjusts triggers, rumble, dead zones and audio. It is officially licensed for Xbox Series X|S, works with Xbox One and Windows 10/11, and connects with a generous 3-metre USB-C cable: wired only, so there is no battery to manage, but no wireless option either.

Key facts:

  • Connectivity: wired USB-C only, with a 3 m (10 ft) cable included
  • Hall Effect thumbstick modules — the triggers are not Hall Effect
  • Quick-Twist thumbsticks with three height settings
  • Two mappable Advanced Gaming Buttons on the back
  • Impulse Triggers plus dual rumble motors; 3.5mm stereo headset jack
  • Officially licensed for Xbox Series X|S; works with Xbox One and Windows 10/11; 2-year limited warranty

Check price on Amazon

The Ares Pro, launched in May 2025, is Cosmic Byte's value flagship: one pad that connects to a PC three ways — a 2.4GHz dongle, Bluetooth, or a USB-C cable — and also works with Android and iOS devices. Cosmic Byte lists both its sticks and its triggers as Hall Effect magnetic sensors, which removes the contact wear that causes drift, along with a 1,000 Hz polling rate for fast response.

Around that core it adds a programmable macro button, a Turbo function with adjustable speed, backlit buttons, a textured anti-slip grip and rumble. Unusually, its 3.5mm audio port works in dongle mode as well as wired. One naming caution: Cosmic Byte also sells a separate model called simply Ares Tri-Mode, so check the exact name on the listing before ordering — parts and dongles are not shared between the two.

  • Hall Effect sticks and triggers (maker-listed)
  • 1,000 Hz polling rate (maker-listed)
  • Programmable macro button; Turbo with speed adjustment
  • 3.5mm audio port usable in dongle and wired modes; backlit buttons
  • Listed for PC, Android and iOS

EvoFox is the gaming brand of Indian peripherals maker Amkette, and the Elite X2 Pro, launched in July 2025, is its most complete pad. Its HallSense magnetic sticks and triggers come with two-step trigger behaviour and a maker-stated 1,000 Hz polling rate, and it connects three ways — 2.4GHz, Bluetooth 5.0 or USB-C — across PC, Android, iOS and Nintendo Switch.

Two programmable back buttons, marked M1 and M2, can carry macros of up to 16 buttons, set up on the pad itself or in EvoFox's KeyLinker app, which also handles remapping, stick and trigger sensitivity, vibration and firmware updates. Key facts:

  • Connectivity: 2.4GHz wireless via USB dongle, up to 10 m range
  • Built-in rechargeable lithium-ion battery

  • Made for Windows PC (the listing states Windows 7, 8, 8.1 and 10)

8. Redgear Pro Wired Gamepad — Best Budget Wired

Check price on Amazon

The Pro Wired is the same Redgear formula minus the battery: a USB cable — at a reasonably long 1.8 metres — is its only connection, which also makes it the one controller here that can never run flat in the middle of a game. It suits a desk set-up, a second player, or a spare pad kept in a drawer.

It keeps the illuminated ABXY buttons and the integrated force feedback of the wireless version, and it supports both XInput and DirectInput, so current Windows games and older titles alike can recognise it. Two analog sticks, two analog triggers and 11 digital keys match the layout PC players expect. As with its wireless sibling, Redgear's listing names Windows 7, 8, 8.1 and 10 — worth knowing if you run something older or newer.

Key facts:

  • Connectivity: wired USB, with a 1.8 m cable
  • Integrated force feedback vibration
  • Illuminated ABXY buttons
  • XInput and DirectInput compatible
  • Two analog sticks, two analog triggers and 11 digital keys
  • Made for Windows PC (the listing states Windows 7, 8, 8.1 and 10)

What About a Dedicated Flight Stick?

If you mainly play Microsoft Flight Simulator, X-Plane, DCS World or a space sim such as Elite Dangerous, a gamepad does work — all of those games support controllers — but a flight stick gives you a longer, finer throw of movement, and a HOTAS set puts a throttle under your other hand as well.

The names worth knowing are Thrustmaster's range — the T.16000M FCS, whose main axes use magnetic Hall sensors, and the T.Flight Hotas One with its detachable throttle — and Logitech's Extreme 3D Pro and X52 systems. We name them for orientation only: flight-sim gear in India is import-driven, stock comes and goes, and prices vary widely between sellers, so no single listing met this guide's standard for a product link. You can search Amazon.in for flight sticks — and buy only from a seller whose returns and warranty terms you have read first.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a PlayStation 5 controller work on a PC?

Yes, and it is straightforward. Pair it with a Windows PC or a Mac over Bluetooth, or plug it in with USB-C; Steam's controller layer then makes it work across most Steam games, and a growing number of Windows releases support it natively. Its haptic feedback and adaptive triggers only work in games that support them, and on PC the full haptics need the USB connection. It does not connect natively to a PS4 console.

What is the difference between XInput and DirectInput?

XInput is Microsoft's controller standard, built around the Xbox layout. Modern Windows games expect it, so an XInput pad works with no set-up at all. DirectInput is the older, more generic standard that XInput replaced; most new games ignore it, but some older titles only speak DirectInput — which is why several pads in this guide can switch between the two modes.

Is wired or wireless better for competitive gaming?

A cable remains the simplest zero-compromise option: no battery, no interference, no pairing. But a 2.4GHz dongle connection on a modern pad, polling at up to 1,000 Hz, feels identical in ordinary play, while Bluetooth is the connection most likely to add noticeable delay. In practice the set-up matters more than the category — if you compete, use a cable or the dongle, and keep Bluetooth for casual and mobile play.

What is stick drift, and do Hall Effect sticks prevent it?

Drift is when a resting stick reports movement it is not making, so your character or camera creeps on its own. In conventional sticks, position is read by a contact wiper moving across a resistive track; that contact wears with use, and the centre reading wanders. Hall Effect sticks read position with a magnet and a sensor that never touch, so that particular wear point does not exist. It does not make a controller immortal — springs, buttons and batteries still age — but it removes the most common cause of drift.

Can I use one of these controllers with my phone or Android TV?

With a phone, often yes: the Xbox controller, the DualSense and the Bluetooth modes of the Cosmic Byte and EvoFox pads all list Android and iOS support. Android TV is patchier and depends on the exact model, so check the product listing for your device before buying. The wired PowerA and the two Redgear pads are aimed at PC use (and Xbox, in the PowerA's case), not at mobile gaming.

Do I need a flight stick to play Microsoft Flight Simulator?

No. Microsoft Flight Simulator fully supports gamepads, and many players fly happily on an Xbox controller. A stick and throttle add finer control and a good deal of immersion, and they become worthwhile if you fly several times a week — but treat them as an upgrade, not a requirement, and read the flight stick section above before buying that hardware in India.

Conclusion

Start with how you play. For one pad that works everywhere on a PC, take the Xbox Wireless Controller; for feel, the DualSense; for wired pro features, the PowerA Advantage Plus; for tri-mode value, the Cosmic Byte Ares Pro or an EvoFox pad with HallSense sticks; and for the tightest budget, a Redgear Pro, wired or wireless. Flight-sim players should read the flight stick section and buy that hardware only from a listing they have checked carefully. Whichever pad fits your desk, its button above leads to the live Amazon.in price — check it, and play.

Prices are not printed because they change too often to stay accurate; check the live price, delivery promise and warranty terms on the product page before you order. Nine very different machines sit under the single label “body massager” in India: percussion guns that tap, shiatsu nodes that knead, foot machines that roll, air sleeves that squeeze and a small scalp massager that rotates. They are not interchangeable, and the right buy depends on which part of the body you want to use it on and how. This guide covers one or two strong examples of each main type, checked against the manufacturer’s own material and its Amazon.in listing in November 2026, with the mechanical facts that actually differ between them.

Prices for these products change frequently with offers and coupons, so this guide prints none; the Check price on Amazon buttons show the live figure on the day you buy. One point of honesty up front: a home massager is a comfort device for relaxation and unwinding. It is not a medical device, it does not diagnose or treat anything, and the sensible-use section below explains where the limits are.

This post contains affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, we earn from qualifying purchases. This does not affect our editorial independence.

Quick Answer

  • First percussion gun, for most people: AGARO Galaxy — cordless, light, four heads and six speeds.
  • Strongest tapping, nothing to charge: AGARO Impact — a corded 80 W gun with six heads.
  • Handheld wand on a budget: AGARO Relaxo — corded, eight heads, made for back, legs and feet.
  • Neck and shoulders while you sit: Dr Physio 1013 — a heated shiatsu wrap with rotating nodes.
  • On a chair or car seat: beatXP Deep Heal Pillow — a shiatsu cushion with heat and a car adaptor in the box.
  • Feet only, kept simple: Lifelong LLM72 — kneading and rolling with four automatic programmes.
  • Feet plus calves: Lifelong LLM99 — a larger four-motor machine with heat.
  • Scalp: Caresmith Revive — a cordless rotating scalp massager with washable heads.
  • Legs, squeeze only: AGARO MAGMA — air-compression sleeves for feet, calves and thighs.

The Main Types of Body Massager, Explained

  • Percussion guns drive a head in and out in rapid taps. The head shape sets the feel: round heads spread the tapping, bullet or cone heads concentrate it on one spot, flat heads cover broad muscles and fork or U-shaped heads work either side of the spine.
  • Handheld wands are the older design — a vibrating, tapping head on a handle, almost always mains-powered. The handle helps you reach your own back, and output is identical from the first minute to the last because there is no battery to fade.
  • Shiatsu wraps put rotating nodes inside a U-shaped wrap worn over the shoulders. The nodes turn in a kneading motion and reverse direction periodically; many models add a heating element.
  • Massage pillows use the same rotating-node mechanism in a cushion you lean against on a sofa, office chair or car seat, so body weight sets the pressure.
  • Foot and leg machines enclose the feet — and on larger models the calves — and combine rollers under the sole with kneading pads at the sides, run as timed automatic programmes.
  • Air-compression sleeves contain airbags that inflate and deflate in sequence, squeezing the leg in waves rather than kneading it. There are no moving massage heads at all.
  • Scalp massagers are small cordless devices whose rotating silicone-tipped heads knead the scalp; the heads detach for washing and can be used with hair oil.

Best Body Massagers in India — Quick Comparison

Best Body Massagers in India — Detailed Reviews

1. AGARO Galaxy Gun Massager

Check price on Amazon

AGARO’s Galaxy is the straightforward starting point in this list: a 595 g cordless percussion gun whose 25 W motor is rated by the manufacturer at up to 3,500 strokes per minute. Four interchangeable heads — round, bullet, flat and fork — cover everything from large leg muscles to either side of the spine, and six speed settings run from gentle to firm. The 4,000 mAh battery is rated for up to three hours of use and charges over Type-C, and a 15-minute auto shut-off ends each session for you.

Key Details

  • Type: Percussion massage gun
  • Power: Battery, 4,000 mAh, Type-C charging
  • Attachments: 4 heads (round, bullet, flat, fork)
  • Speed settings: 6
  • Motor: 25 W, up to 3,500 strokes per minute (manufacturer rating)
  • Auto shut-off: 15 minutes
  • Weight: 595 g

2. AGARO Impact Gun Massager

Check price on Amazon

The Impact takes the opposite approach to the Galaxy: it plugs into the mains, so its 80 W motor delivers up to 4,000 vibrations per minute at full strength for as long as you use it, with nothing to recharge. Six heads — standard ball, flat, U-shaped, cone, big ball and arc — give the widest head selection in this guide, across five speed settings. At 850 g it is heavier than the battery guns, and the cord decides where you can use it, but for a fixed spot at home it is the strongest tapping action here.

Key Details

  • Type: Percussion massage gun
  • Power: Corded electric, 80 W motor
  • Attachments: 6 heads (ball, flat, U-shape, cone, big ball, arc)
  • Speed settings: 5
  • Output: Up to 4,000 vibrations per minute (manufacturer rating)
  • Weight: 850 g

3. AGARO Relaxo Electric Handheld Massager

Check price on Amazon

The Relaxo is a corded handheld wand built for reaching your own back, legs and feet. Eight detachable heads change the contact surface, and five vibration modes combined with six speed settings give more combinations than most wands offer. A cloth mesh cover sits over the head to stop hair tangling as it works, controls are simple finger-touch buttons, and the unit switches itself off after 15 minutes. At 1.25 kg it is the heaviest handheld here, which matters on long sessions; in short ones it is a lot of coverage for the format.

Key Details

  • Type: Handheld wand massager
  • Power: Corded electric
  • Attachments: 8 detachable heads
  • Settings: 5 vibration modes, 6 speeds
  • Auto shut-off: 15 minutes
  • Cover: Cloth mesh, to reduce hair tangling
  • Weight: 1.25 kg
  • Warranty: 1 year (manufacturer)

4. Dr Physio (USA) Electric Heat Shiatsu Massager 1013

Check price on Amazon

Dr Physio’s 1013 is the wrap style of shiatsu massager: it sits over the neck and shoulders while eight bi-directional rotating nodes knead, reversing direction automatically, with three speed settings. A heating function warms as it works, which the manufacturer caps at 40 degrees Celsius through infrared bulbs. It runs from a mains adaptor and also includes a car adaptor, and an auto shut-off ends the session. The same wrap can be positioned against the lower back or legs, which makes it more flexible than its neck-and-shoulder name suggests.

Key Details

  • Type: Shiatsu neck and shoulder wrap
  • Nodes: 8 bi-directional rotating nodes
  • Speed settings: 3, with auto-rotation direction change
  • Heat: Infrared, up to 40°C (manufacturer figure)
  • Power: Corded, AC adaptor and car adaptor included
  • Auto shut-off: Yes
  • Weight: 1.9 kg

5. beatXP Deep Heal Pillow Massager

Check price on Amazon

The Deep Heal Pillow puts four bi-directional shiatsu rollers inside a cushion you lean back on, so your own body weight sets the pressure. A single button cycles its three modes — clockwise, anti-clockwise and heating — and the infrared heat reaches 40 degrees Celsius. The pure copper motor is rated at 3,000 RPM by the manufacturer. Home and car adaptors are both in the box, a 15-minute auto shut-off ends each session, and at 1.35 kg it moves easily between a sofa, a desk chair and a car seat.

Key Details

  • Type: Shiatsu massage pillow
  • Rollers: 4 bi-directional rollers
  • Modes: 3 (clockwise, anti-clockwise, heating), single-button control
  • Heat: Infrared, up to 40°C (manufacturer figure)
  • Motor: Pure copper, rated 3,000 RPM (manufacturer figure)
  • Power: Corded, home and car adaptors included
  • Auto shut-off: 15 minutes
  • Weight: 1.35 kg

6. Lifelong LLM72 Foot Massager

Check price on Amazon

The LLM72 is a floor-standing foot massager that works on both feet at once with flexible rubber kneading pads and a rolling action under the soles. Four automatic programmes run the session for you, or you can pick from three custom modes; a remote control is included, so you never have to bend down to change settings mid-session. The 40 W motor runs from the mains and the machine switches off automatically after 15 minutes. It covers feet only — for calves as well, look at the LLM99 below.

Key Details

  • Type: Foot massager (kneading and rolling)
  • Programmes: 4 automatic programmes, 3 custom modes
  • Power: Corded, 40 W, AC 220–240 V
  • Control: Remote control included
  • Auto shut-off: 15 minutes
  • Warranty: 1 year, extendable by 6 months on registration (manufacturer scheme)

7. Lifelong LLM99 Foot, Calf and Leg Massager

Check price on Amazon

The LLM99 is the big-machine option: your feet and calves sit inside it together, and four motors drive kneading, rolling, vibration and heating modes. Three automatic programmes and three personal programmes are selected on an LED display, and the fabric covers are removable for washing, which matters on a machine the whole household may use. It is a substantial 10.4 kg unit that will live in one corner of a room rather than travel, and a 15-minute auto shut-off ends every session.

Key Details

  • Type: Foot, calf and leg massager
  • Motors: 4 motors, 80 W total
  • Modes: Kneading, rolling, vibration, heating
  • Programmes: 3 automatic, 3 personal, LED display
  • Power: Corded, AC 220–240 V
  • Auto shut-off: 15 minutes
  • Covers: Removable fabric covers for cleaning
  • Weight: 10.4 kg
  • Warranty: 1 year (brand)

8. Caresmith Revive Scalp Massager

Check price on Amazon

The Revive is the specialist in this list: a palm-sized cordless massager whose four rotating heads carry 96 soft silicone kneading points that work across the scalp. Three modes — Regular, Deep and Pulsating — change the rotation pattern. The heads detach for washing and, as the brand positions it, can be used with hair oil during a session. It is USB-rechargeable, and Caresmith rates the battery at up to seven days of use per charge, so it travels well. The same heads can be run over the neck and shoulders at a gentler intensity.

Key Details

  • Type: Electric scalp massager
  • Heads: 4 rotating heads, 96 silicone kneading points
  • Modes: 3 (Regular, Deep, Pulsating)
  • Power: Cordless, USB rechargeable
  • Battery: Up to 7 days per charge (brand rating)
  • Heads detach for washing; can be used with hair oil

9. AGARO MAGMA Air Compression Leg Massager

Check price on Amazon

The MAGMA works completely differently from everything above it: two sleeves wrap around the feet, calves and thighs, and airbags inside them inflate and deflate to squeeze the legs in sequence. A wired handheld controller selects three modes — Sequence, Circulation and Whole — and three intensities, low, medium and high. AGARO lists the model in its current range, and an automatic shut-off ends the session after 20 minutes. There are no kneading heads or rollers at all, which makes it the gentlest-feeling option here for tired legs at the end of the day.

Key Details

  • Type: Air-compression leg massager
  • Coverage: Feet, calves and thighs, both legs
  • Modes: 3 (Sequence, Circulation, Whole)
  • Intensities: 3 (low, medium, high)
  • Control: Wired handheld controller
  • In the box: 2 massage sleeves, controller, power adaptor
  • Auto shut-off: 20 minutes
  • Weight: 1.55 kg
  • Warranty: 1 year (manufacturer)

How to Choose a Body Massager in India

  • Start with the body part. Guns and wands go where you point them; wraps, pillows, foot machines and sleeves only work on the area they are shaped for. Buy for the area you will actually use most.
  • Then the mechanism. Tapping (percussion), kneading (rotating nodes), rolling, vibration and air squeezing all feel different. If you dislike strong tapping, a shiatsu or air-compression model is the safer direction.
  • Corded or cordless is a real trade-off. Corded models hold full output indefinitely and are often cheaper; cordless models move around the house and travel, at the cost of charging and a heavier battery in the hand.
  • Treat headline speeds with care. Strokes or vibrations per minute describe how fast a head moves, not how deep it presses. Head shape, motor torque and how much pressure you apply matter as much as the speed figure.
  • Check the timer. Every model here switches itself off after 15 or 20 minutes. That is a sensible built-in session limit, not a restriction to work around.
  • Plan for cleaning and storage. Detachable heads, mesh covers and washable fabric all make a shared household machine more pleasant to live with.

What the Specifications Mean

  • Strokes or vibrations per minute — how many times the head taps in a minute at a given speed setting. Higher is more intense-feeling, not automatically better.
  • Speed settings and modes — speeds change how fast the head moves; modes change the pattern (rotation direction on shiatsu models, inflation sequence on air sleeves). Pattern changes are often more noticeable than one extra speed.
  • Heads and attachments — on guns and wands these swap the contact shape. A fork head straddles the spine rather than pressing on it; a bullet concentrates force, so use it gently and briefly.
  • Heat figures — where a manufacturer gives a temperature (40°C on both heated models here), that is the surface warmth the element is capped at, stated by the brand, not a treatment dose.
  • Battery capacity (mAh) — higher generally means longer cordless use, but the manufacturer’s own hours-per-charge figure is the number to compare, since motor draw varies.
  • Watts — on corded models this is power draw. It hints at motor size but does not by itself tell you how a massage will feel.

Using a Massager Sensibly

These devices are sold for relaxation and comfort. Used with a little restraint they are simple household appliances; used carelessly — pressed hard into the neck, run for an hour, or used over an injury — they can bruise and aggravate. A few ground rules cover every type in this guide.

  • Keep sessions to the built-in timer — 15 to 20 minutes per area is the limit the manufacturers themselves set with their auto shut-offs.
  • Never run a percussion gun over the front or side of the neck, the spine itself, joints, the head, or broken or inflamed skin. Fork heads are shaped to work either side of the spine, not on it.
  • Start on the lowest setting with any new device and increase gradually. More intensity is not more benefit.
  • Stop if you feel pain, numbness, tingling or dizziness, and do not use a massager over a recent injury, fracture or surgical site.
  • Ask a doctor before use if you are pregnant, have a pacemaker or other implant, have varicose veins or a history of blood clots (this matters most for air-compression sleeves), or have any condition affecting circulation or sensation.
  • A massager is not a substitute for medical care. Persistent pain is a reason to see a doctor or physiotherapist, not to buy a stronger machine.

FAQs

Which type of body massager is best for the back?

For the back specifically, a percussion gun or a handheld wand is the practical choice because you — or someone helping you — can place it where you want; a fork head works either side of the spine. A shiatsu pillow works for the lower back while seated, since you lean against it. Fixed machines for feet and legs cannot reach the back at all.

How long should one massage session be?

Follow the device: every model in this guide switches itself off after 15 minutes, or 20 minutes for the AGARO MAGMA sleeves, and that timer is a sensible session length for one area. If you want to cover several areas, move the device rather than restarting it repeatedly on the same spot.

Corded or cordless — which is better?

Neither, outright. Corded models such as the AGARO Impact and Relaxo give full output for as long as they run and never need charging, but tether you to a socket. Cordless models such as the AGARO Galaxy and Caresmith Revive move freely around the house and travel well, in exchange for charging time and some weight in the hand.

Can a body massager replace medical treatment?

No. These are comfort and relaxation devices, not medical devices, and none of them diagnoses or treats a condition. Brands market them for unwinding and post-exercise routines; if you have ongoing pain or a diagnosed problem, a doctor or physiotherapist is the right route, and a massager is at most an addition they may suggest.

Can I use a foot massager every day?

The foot machines here are built around timed 15-minute programmes, and a daily session within that timer is how the manufacturers present them. Keep the intensity comfortable, give sore feet a rest day if they feel tender, and check with a doctor first if you have diabetes or reduced sensation in your feet, since you may not feel excessive pressure.

What does the speed of a massage gun actually change?

The speed setting changes how many times per minute the head taps — the AGARO Galaxy’s motor is rated up to 3,500 strokes per minute and the corded Impact up to 4,000. It does not change how deep the head travels; that is fixed by the machine’s design. In practice, higher speeds feel more intense on the same muscle, which is why starting low and stepping up is the sensible order.

Conclusion

Match the mechanism to the job and any of these nine will do what it promises mechanically: the AGARO Galaxy as the all-round first gun, the Impact where there is a socket and you want maximum tapping, the two shiatsu models for seated neck, shoulder and back sessions, the Lifelong pair for feet with or without calves, the MAGMA sleeves for a gentle squeeze, and the Caresmith Revive for the scalp. Use the buttons to check the live price, keep sessions inside the built-in timers, and treat every one of them as a comfort device rather than a cure.

Prices and availability change frequently, so this guide deliberately does not print prices — please check the current price on the product page or in your local store.

India's freezer cabinets hold far more than the two or three national names of a generation ago. Dairy cooperatives, century-old family firms, a global parlour chain and venture-backed start-ups now compete for the same shopper, and each brand in this guide has a distinct story behind it.

This guide profiles 12 ice cream brands sold in India today, from Amul's cooperative giant to HOCCO, the newest name in the cabinet. Every profile is based on fresh research checked in November 2026. Prices are not listed, because pack prices vary by city, retailer and season; the pack itself is always the reliable source.

Quick Answer: The 12 Brands at a Glance

  • Amul — the cooperative giant from Anand, Gujarat; everyday tubs, cones, cups and kulfi sold across India.
  • Mother Dairy — the NDDB-owned Delhi brand; a North India staple with a strong kulfi and classics range.
  • Kwality Wall's — home of Cornetto and Magnum; since December 2025 a standalone listed company, majority-owned by The Magnum Ice Cream Company.
  • Vadilal — Ahmedabad's 1907 soda-fountain business, now a listed company known for cassata and a wide flavour range.
  • Havmor — founded in Karachi in 1944, rebuilt in Ahmedabad, owned by South Korea's Lotte since 2017.
  • Naturals Ice Cream — the Mumbai parlour brand built on real fruit, milk and sugar since 1984.
  • Baskin Robbins — the American parlour chain, in India since 1993 through master franchisee Graviss Foods.
  • Arun Icecreams — Chennai's South India favourite, the flagship brand of Hatsun Agro.
  • Dinshaw's — Nagpur's family dairy making ice cream since 1932, strongest across central India.
  • NIC Honestly Crafted — Pune's delivery-era brand from Walko Food Company, known for fruit and Indian-sweet flavours.
  • HOCCO — the Chona family's comeback brand, launched in Ahmedabad in 2023 after the family sold Havmor.
  • Dairy Day — Bengaluru's Dairy Classic brand, a Karnataka and Tamil Nadu regular since 2003.

Ice Cream or Frozen Dessert? The Label That Matters

India's food regulator, FSSAI, keeps two separate legal categories. A product can only be called ice cream if its fat comes from milk; standard ice cream must contain at least 10 per cent milk fat. A similar product made with edible vegetable oil or fat instead must be sold as a frozen dessert, with a boxed declaration on the pack saying it is made with edible vegetable oil or vegetable fat.

Neither category is automatically better — it is a question of taste, ingredients and price — but the distinction explains much of the rivalry in this guide. Amul campaigns on "real milk, real ice cream", while several rivals sell a mix of both types. Many brands here sell ice cream in one line and frozen desserts in another, so the check has to happen pack by pack.

  • Look at the product name first: "ice cream" means milk fat; "frozen dessert" means vegetable fat is used.
  • Read the boxed declaration: frozen desserts must state that they are made with edible vegetable oil or fat.
  • Check the ingredients list: it names the actual fat source, whether cream and milk or a vegetable oil such as palm oil.
  • Do not judge by brand alone: one brand can sell both categories in different packs.

How to Choose an Ice Cream Brand

  • For milk-fat purists: pick packs labelled ice cream, and start with the dairy-led brands — Amul, Arun, Havmor and Mother Dairy.
  • For fruit flavours: Naturals and NIC build their menus around real Indian fruit; Vadilal also runs a deep fruit range.
  • For kulfi: Mother Dairy, Arun and Dinshaw's all treat kulfi as a signature line rather than an afterthought.
  • For a parlour outing: Baskin Robbins and Naturals sell the scoop experience; Havmor's parlours are a western-India institution.
  • For premium sticks and cones: Kwality Wall's carries Magnum and Cornetto, the two global names in this space.
  • For regional favourites: Dinshaw's in central India, Dairy Day in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and HOCCO in Gujarat reward local loyalty.
  • For delivery: NIC built its business on food-delivery and quick-commerce apps, and most big brands now list there too.

The Brands in Detail

1. Amul

Amul is the ice cream arm of India's best-known dairy cooperative. The brand is marketed by the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF) from Anand, the apex body of Gujarat's district milk unions. The cooperative movement behind Amul began in 1946; ice cream arrived much later, launched in Gujarat on 10 March 1996 and rolled out nationally by the end of the decade.

Amul built its ice cream business on a simple pitch: ice cream made from milk, sold at cooperative prices. The range covers tubs, cones, cups, sticks and kulfi in everyday flavours, alongside sugar-free and probiotic lines the brand introduced early. Distribution is the brand's real strength — the same network that delivers Amul milk and butter stocks ice cream in towns of every size.

  • Owner: GCMMF, the Gujarat dairy cooperative federation
  • Headquarters: Anand, Gujarat
  • Ice cream launched: 1996 (the cooperative dates to 1946)
  • Known for: value-priced tubs, cones and kulfi with nationwide reach

Check Amul ice cream on Amazon

2. Mother Dairy

Mother Dairy was commissioned in 1974 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB), set up under Operation Flood, the programme that made India milk-sufficient. The company, Mother Dairy Fruit & Vegetable Pvt Ltd, is based in Delhi and sells milk, curd, paneer, ghee and ice cream under the Mother Dairy name.

In the north, its ice cream is a household staple: classic tubs and bricks, a wide kulfi range and seasonal specials. The company also localises flavours by region; in the east it sells nolen gur (date palm jaggery) ice cream and kulfi, flavours it pioneered in packaged form. Mother Dairy has no brand image in this guide because none was available from an official source.

  • Owner: NDDB (wholly owned subsidiary)
  • Commissioned: 1974, under Operation Flood
  • Base: Delhi
  • Known for: kulfi, classic tubs and regional flavours such as nolen gur

Check Mother Dairy ice cream on Amazon

3. Kwality Wall's

Kwality Wall's has been through the biggest change of any brand in this guide. The brand was created in the mid-1990s by combining the Indian Kwality business with Unilever's Wall's, and it spent three decades inside Hindustan Unilever. On 1 December 2025 the ice cream business was demerged into a standalone company, Kwality Wall's (India) Limited, which listed on the stock exchanges in February 2026.

The Mumbai-based company's majority owner is now The Magnum Ice Cream Company, Unilever's spun-off global ice cream business, which holds a 61.9 per cent stake. Under the Kwality Wall's umbrella sit Cornetto cones, Magnum bars and Feast sticks. The range mixes milk-based ice creams with frozen desserts, so the label check described above matters with this brand.

  • Owner: Kwality Wall's (India) Ltd; The Magnum Ice Cream Company holds 61.9 per cent
  • Headquarters: Mumbai
  • Recent change: demerged from Hindustan Unilever, effective 1 December 2025; listed February 2026
  • Known for: Cornetto, Magnum and Feast

4. Vadilal

Vadilal is the oldest name in this guide. Vadilal Gandhi opened a small soda fountain in Ahmedabad in 1907 and began selling handcrafted ice cream there; his son Ranchhodlal opened the first Vadilal Soda Fountain outlet in 1926 and imported ice cream machinery from Germany. The business today is Vadilal Industries Limited, a listed company still run from Ahmedabad.

The brand is associated with cassata, the layered slice it helped popularise in India, and with one of the widest flavour ranges in the country. Alongside its Indian business, the company says its Vadilal Quick Treat range is sold in more than 45 countries, aimed largely at the Indian diaspora.

  • Owner: Vadilal Industries Limited (listed on BSE and NSE)
  • Founded: 1907, Ahmedabad, by Vadilal Gandhi
  • Known for: cassata and a very wide flavour range
  • International: the company says its Quick Treat range sells in more than 45 countries

5. Havmor

Havmor began as "Have More", an ice cream shop Satish Chona opened in Karachi in 1944. After Partition the family rebuilt the business in Ahmedabad, and over the following decades Havmor became the defining ice cream brand of Gujarat and much of western India, built on parlours and a promise of pure-milk ice cream.

In 2017 South Korea's Lotte Confectionery bought the entire business for a reported ₹1,020 crore, its entry into Indian ice cream. Lotte has since merged Havmor with its other Indian arm, Lotte India, into a single company, with Havmor continuing as a brand. Production runs from plants in Gujarat, Haryana and Maharashtra.

  • Owner: the Lotte group of South Korea, which bought the business in 2017
  • Founded: 1944, Karachi; rebuilt in Ahmedabad after Partition
  • Headquarters: Ahmedabad
  • Known for: parlours and a strong western-India presence

6. Naturals Ice Cream

Naturals is the parlour brand that proved Indian fruit could carry an ice cream menu. Raghunandan Srinivas Kamath, the son of a Mangaluru mango seller, opened the first shop in Juhu, Mumbai, on 14 February 1984. His rule was simple: ice cream made from fruit, milk and sugar, without artificial flavouring standing in for the fruit itself.

Seasonal fruit flavours remain the draw: mango, sitaphal (custard apple), jackfruit, tender coconut and chikoo, several of them available only while the fruit is in season. Kamath died in 2024, but the family company, Kamaths Ourtimes Ice Creams, continues to run a network of well over a hundred parlours. The brand has also been named among the world's most iconic ice creams by TasteAtlas.

  • Owner: Kamaths Ourtimes Ice Creams Pvt Ltd
  • Founded: 1984, Juhu, Mumbai, by Raghunandan Srinivas Kamath
  • Made with: fruit, milk and sugar, per the brand's stated method
  • Known for: seasonal Indian fruit flavours, served in parlours

7. Baskin Robbins

Baskin Robbins is the only global chain in this guide. It was founded in California in 1945 by brothers-in-law Burt Baskin and Irv Robbins, and built its name on variety — its original promise was 31 flavours, one for every day of the month. The brand is now part of Inspire Brands in the United States.

India came in 1993, when Mumbai's Graviss Group took the master franchise for India and the SAARC region and opened the first store in Mumbai. The ice cream is made locally at a plant near Pune. The chain's 1,000th store in the region opened in Andheri, Mumbai, in September 2024, and the company says the network has since grown past 1,100 parlours.

  • Global owner: Inspire Brands; the brand was founded in 1945 in California, USA
  • India operator: Graviss Foods, master franchisee since 1993
  • First Indian store: Mumbai, 1993
  • Known for: rotating international flavours and the parlour experience

8. Arun Icecreams

Arun is the South's home-grown giant. R. G. Chandramogan started it in 1970, aged 21, making ice candies in a rented 250 square foot space in Royapuram, Chennai, with about ₹13,000 raised from selling family property. The venture grew into Hatsun Agro Product Limited, today described as India's largest private-sector dairy company, with Arun as its flagship brand.

The range leans on milk and cream: tubs, cones, sticks and a much-loved malai kulfi line, sold through parlours and retail freezers across the southern states. Hatsun also runs Ibaco, a premium scoop brand launched in 2012. In 2026 Arun stepped outside India, making its United States debut at New York's India Day Parade.

  • Owner: Hatsun Agro Product Limited (listed), Chennai
  • Founded: 1970, Chennai, by R. G. Chandramogan
  • Known for: kulfi and everyday milk-based ice cream in South India
  • Sister brand: Ibaco, the premium parlour brand launched in 2012

9. Dinshaw's

Dinshaw's has been making ice cream in Nagpur since before Independence. Brothers Dinshaw and Erachshaw Rana started a small dairy at Gittikhadan, Nagpur, in 1932, selling milk, curd and hand-churned ice cream. The hand churners gave way to freezers in the 1950s, as the brothers worked to extend ice cream eating beyond the summer months.

The company, Dinshaw's Dairy Foods, is still family-owned, by the Rana and Bapuna families, and ice cream remains about half its business, alongside dairy products, bakery items and namkeen. Its strength is central India — Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and neighbouring states. In 2025 the 93-year-old brand gave itself a complete makeover, with new packaging and identity.

  • Owner: Dinshaw's Dairy Foods (the Rana and Bapuna families)
  • Founded: 1932, Nagpur, by Dinshaw and Erachshaw Rana
  • Known for: kulfi and classics across central India
  • Update: a complete brand makeover in 2025

10. NIC Honestly Crafted

NIC is the youngest big name here, built for the delivery-app era. Its parent, Walko Food Company, was founded in Pune in 2012 by Jeetendra Bhandari, Sanjiv Shah and Raj Bhandari, and the NIC brand was launched in 2015. The pitch is in the name: honestly crafted ice cream made with milk, without artificial colours or flavours.

Fruit and Indian-sweet flavours lead the menu — Alphonso mango, sitaphal, tender coconut and mithai-inspired tubs — and the brand sells heavily through food-delivery and quick-commerce platforms as well as its own outlets. Investors noticed: Walko raised $11 million in a 2023 funding round led by Jungle Ventures. Its sister brands include Grameen Kulfi and Café Chokolade.

  • Owner: Walko Food Company Pvt Ltd, Pune (founded 2012)
  • Founders: Jeetendra Bhandari, Sanjiv Shah and Raj Bhandari
  • Funding: an $11 million round led by Jungle Ventures in 2023
  • Known for: fruit and Indian-sweet flavours, and a strong delivery-app presence

11. HOCCO

HOCCO is a famous ice cream family starting again. The Chonas of Ahmedabad founded Havmor in 1944 and sold it to Lotte in 2017. Once the sale's non-compete period ended, Ankit Chona brought the family back into ice cream under a new name: HOCCO, short for House of Chonas Collaborative, which began commercial operations in October 2023 from a new plant at Bavla, near Ahmedabad.

HOCCO targets the mass market with cups, cones, sticks and tubs, while the family's premium label Huber & Holly — launched in 2016 and kept out of the Lotte sale — continues in parlours and packaged retail. The comeback is well funded: the company raised ₹100 crore in a 2026 funding round led by existing investor Sauce.vc.

  • Owner: HOCCO (House of Chonas Collaborative), Ahmedabad
  • Founder: Ankit Chona, of the family behind Havmor
  • Commercial launch: October 2023
  • Premium sibling: Huber & Holly

12. Dairy Day

Dairy Day is Bengaluru's contribution to this guide. Dairy Classic Ice Creams Private Limited was incorporated in 2002 and established the Dairy Day brand in 2003; the company was founded by a team of professionals who left multinational jobs to make ice cream. Manufacturing is centralised near Bengaluru.

The brand's heartland is Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, where it sells tubs, cones, cups and frozen desserts through a wide retail network. In 2016 Motilal Oswal Private Equity invested ₹110 crore for a minority stake, to fund capacity and distribution growth — a sign of how seriously investors take strong regional brands.

  • Owner: Dairy Classic Ice Creams Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru
  • Established: 2003 (the company was incorporated in 2002)
  • Backing: Motilal Oswal Private Equity took a minority stake in 2016
  • Known for: an everyday range across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu

Brand Comparison Table

BrandOwner / companyBaseRootsBest known for
AmulGCMMF (dairy cooperative)Anand, Gujarat1946; ice cream from 1996Everyday value range, nationwide
Mother DairyNDDB subsidiaryDelhi1974Kulfi and northern classics

VadilalVadilal Industries LtdAhmedabad1907Cassata, wide flavour range
HavmorLotte groupAhmedabad1944Parlours, western-India strength
NaturalsKamaths Ourtimes Ice CreamsMumbai1984Real-fruit parlour flavours
Baskin RobbinsInspire Brands; Graviss Foods in IndiaMumbai (India)1945; India from 1993Rotating global flavours
Arun IcecreamsHatsun Agro Product LtdChennai1970Kulfi and southern everyday range
Dinshaw'sDinshaw's Dairy FoodsNagpur1932Central-India family favourite
NICWalko Food CompanyPune2012; NIC from 2015Fruit and mithai flavours, delivery-first

Roots show when the company or brand began. Amul's cooperative dates to 1946 but entered ice cream in 1996; Baskin Robbins began in the United States in 1945 and entered India in 1993.

Storage and Serving Tips

  • Keep it at −18°C or colder: a home freezer's coldest setting keeps texture firm and slows ice crystals.
  • Refreeze carefully: melted ice cream that is refrozen turns icy; serve what you need and return the tub quickly.
  • Rest before scooping: five to ten minutes at room temperature softens a hard tub without melting it.
  • Seal the surface: pressing cling film onto the surface of an opened tub limits freezer burn.
  • Mind the date: check the manufacturing and best-before dates on the pack, especially on slow-moving flavours.

FAQs

Which is the best ice cream brand in India?

There is no single answer. Amul leads on reach and value, Kwality Wall's on global stick and cone brands, Naturals and NIC on fruit flavours, and regional brands such as Arun, Dinshaw's and Dairy Day often beat the nationals in their home states. The best choice depends on the flavour, format and label type you prefer.

What is the difference between ice cream and a frozen dessert?

Under FSSAI rules, ice cream must be made with milk fat, while a frozen dessert may use edible vegetable oil or fat instead. Both contain milk solids. A frozen dessert pack must carry a declaration that it is made with edible vegetable oil or fat, so the front and back of the pack tell you which type you are buying.

Which brands are best for kulfi?

Mother Dairy, Arun and Dinshaw's all treat kulfi as a core line, with malai and flavoured variants sold widely in their regions. Walko, NIC's parent, also runs a dedicated kulfi brand, Grameen Kulfi. Amul and Vadilal sell kulfi nationally as part of their stick ranges.

Which brand should I choose for fruit flavours?

Naturals is the specialist: its menu is built around seasonal Indian fruit made with milk and sugar. NIC runs a similar fruit-led list, including Alphonso mango and sitaphal, and Vadilal offers one of the widest fruit ranges among the national brands.

Are these brands vegetarian?

Ice cream sold in India is almost always vegetarian, and packs carry the green dot mark to confirm it. A small number of premium or imported-style flavours can contain egg, so if that matters to you, check the ingredients list and the veg mark on the specific pack.

Why does this guide not list prices?

Pack prices change with the season, the city and the retailer, and promotional pricing on delivery apps changes faster still. Any printed price would mislead within weeks, so this guide compares brands on ownership, range and strengths instead, and leaves the price check to the pack in front of you.

Conclusion

India's ice cream market rewards every kind of maker: the cooperative scale of Amul and Mother Dairy, the heritage of Vadilal and Dinshaw's, the parlour craft of Naturals and Baskin Robbins, and the energy of newcomers such as NIC and HOCCO. Ownership keeps changing — Kwality Wall's is newly independent, Havmor is Korean-owned, and the family that sold Havmor is competing again — but the freezer cabinet keeps getting more interesting.

Choose by the label first (ice cream or frozen dessert), then by the flavour you actually want, and let regional loyalty have its say. Whichever of these 12 brands you pick, you are buying from a company with a real story behind it.
