title.rendered: Most Influential Women in the World: 15 Women Who Changed History

content.rendered:
Fifteen women, fifteen very different kinds of power. A physicist who won Nobel Prizes in two sciences, a pilot who vanished over the Pacific, a seamstress whose arrest changed American law, a painter whose work now holds an auction record, heads of government, a saint, a tennis champion who came back, and a schoolgirl who survived a gunman and won the Nobel Peace Prize. This guide explains, for each of them, what she actually did and why it still matters.

The list is an editorial selection, not an official ranking, and it is ordered by theme rather than by importance. Every entry was re-researched for this edition in November 2026: dates and achievements were checked against institutional and reference sources, and the current position of every living woman on the list was verified, because several of their stories have moved on in the last two years.

Quick Answer: The 15 Women at a Glance

  • Marie Curie — the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
  • Amelia Earhart — the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic.
  • Rosa Parks — her refusal to give up a bus seat sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.
  • Frida Kahlo — the Mexican painter whose self-portraits became global icons.
  • Indira Gandhi — India’s first and so far only woman prime minister.
  • Mother Teresa — founder of the Missionaries of Charity and Nobel Peace laureate.
  • Jane Goodall — the primatologist who transformed our understanding of chimpanzees.
  • Angela Merkel — Chancellor of Germany for 16 years and Europe’s crisis manager.
  • Oprah Winfrey — the talk-show host who built a media empire she owned herself.
  • Serena Williams — winner of 23 Grand Slam singles titles and a venture investor.
  • Ursula von der Leyen — President of the European Commission, now in a second term.
  • Kamala Harris — the first woman to serve as Vice President of the United States.
  • Jacinda Ardern — New Zealand’s prime minister at 37, known for empathetic leadership.
  • Malala Yousafzai — the youngest Nobel laureate in history, for girls’ education.
  • Nirmala Sitharaman — India’s finance minister, presenter of a record nine straight Budgets.

Science and Exploration: Curie, Earhart and Goodall

1. Marie Curie

Marie Curie, born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, moved to Paris for the education her home country denied women, and there, working with her husband Pierre, she turned the new phenomenon of radiation into a science. She coined the term radioactivity, and in 1898 the Curies announced two new elements: polonium, named for her occupied homeland, and radium.

The honours have never been matched. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911, and remains the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences. Widowed in 1906, she took Pierre’s chair at the Sorbonne, the first woman to hold one. In the First World War she took X-ray units to the front line. She died in 1934 of an illness her doctors linked to decades of radiation exposure.

  • Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Poland; died 4 July 1934, France.
  • Field: Physics and chemistry.
  • Defining achievement: Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, a feat no one has repeated.
  • Legacy: Her research underpins radiation medicine and nuclear science to this day.

2. Amelia Earhart

Amelia Earhart became famous in 1928 as the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air, as a passenger, and honest enough to call herself “a sack of potatoes” on that flight. Four years later she made the crossing alone. On 20–21 May 1932 she flew a Lockheed Vega from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in about 15 hours, fighting ice, fatigue and a leaking fuel tank, and landed in a farmer’s field.

She used the fame deliberately, co-founding the Ninety-Nines organisation of women pilots and campaigning for women’s place in aviation. In 1937 she set out to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan. On 2 July, on the long Pacific leg to Howland Island, her radio messages faded and stopped. Neither the aircraft nor its crew was ever found, and the disappearance remains unsolved.

  • Born: 24 July 1897, Atchison, Kansas; disappeared 2 July 1937 over the Pacific.
  • Field: Aviation.
  • Defining achievement: First woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic (1932).
  • Legacy: A lasting symbol of women entering professions closed to them.

3. Jane Goodall

Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe, in what is now Tanzania, in 1960, a 26-year-old with no university degree, sent by the anthropologist Louis Leakey to watch chimpanzees. Within months she had seen a chimpanzee, David Greybeard, strip leaves from a twig to fish for termites: tool-making, then believed to be uniquely human. Her patient, decades-long study redrew the boundary between humans and other animals.

In 1977 she founded the Jane Goodall Institute, and in 1991 the Roots & Shoots youth programme, shifting her own work from research to worldwide conservation campaigning. She was still touring and speaking in her nineties. Goodall died on 1 October 2025, aged 91, in Los Angeles during a speaking tour; the institute she founded continues her work, and April 3 is now marked as Jane Goodall Day.

  • Born: 3 April 1934, London; died 1 October 2025, Los Angeles.
  • Field: Primatology and conservation.
  • Defining achievement: The Gombe chimpanzee studies that transformed primatology.
  • Legacy: The Jane Goodall Institute and Roots & Shoots continue her work around the world.

Conscience and Civil Rights: Parks, Mother Teresa and Malala

4. Rosa Parks

On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks, a seamstress and the secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, finished her working day, boarded a city bus, and refused the driver’s order to give her seat to a white passenger. Her arrest for breaking Alabama’s segregation laws was planned for by no one, but a movement was ready for it: Montgomery’s Black community boycotted the buses for 381 days.

The boycott, led by the young Martin Luther King Jr, ended only when the United States Supreme Court upheld a ruling that segregated bus seating was unconstitutional. Parks, often called the mother of the civil rights movement, kept working for the cause for the rest of her life. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996 and died in Detroit in 2005, the first woman to lie in honour in the United States Capitol rotunda.

  • Born: 4 February 1913, Tuskegee, Alabama; died 24 October 2005, Detroit.
  • Field: Civil rights.
  • Defining achievement: Her 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.
  • Legacy: A foundational figure of the American civil rights movement.

5. Mother Teresa

Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, born in Skopje in 1910, joined the Sisters of Loreto and was sent to India, where she taught in a Calcutta school for nearly twenty years. In 1946, on a train journey, she felt what she called a “call within a call”: to leave the convent and live among the poorest people in the city’s slums. In 1950 she founded her own order, the Missionaries of Charity.

The order grew from one woman in a slum to more than 4,000 sisters running hospices, orphanages and homes for the dying around the world by the time of her death in 1997. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and India’s Bharat Ratna in 1980. Pope Francis canonised her as Saint Teresa of Calcutta on 4 September 2016.

  • Born: 26 August 1910, Skopje (now North Macedonia); died 5 September 1997, Calcutta.
  • Field: Humanitarian and religious work.
  • Defining achievement: Founding the Missionaries of Charity in 1950.
  • Legacy: Nobel Peace laureate and a canonised saint of the Catholic Church.

6. Malala Yousafzai

Malala Yousafzai was eleven when she began writing an anonymous BBC blog about life under the Taliban in Pakistan’s Swat Valley, where militants were closing girls’ schools. Her identity became public, and on 9 October 2012 a Taliban gunman shot the fifteen-year-old on her school bus. Flown to Birmingham for treatment, she recovered, and refused to stop: “I tell my story not because it is unique, but because it is the story of many girls.”

In 2013 she co-founded the Malala Fund with her father Ziauddin. In 2014 she became, at seventeen, the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate in history. She went on to read Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Oxford, graduating in 2020. Her memoir Finding My Way, published in October 2025, describes those Oxford years frankly, and the Malala Fund continues its work, including emergency education grants after Pakistan’s 2025 floods.

  • Born: 12 July 1997, Mingora, Swat Valley, Pakistan.
  • Field: Education activism.
  • Defining achievement: The youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate, at 17.
  • Current role: Co-founder of the Malala Fund; author of Finding My Way (2025).

Art, Media and Sport: Kahlo, Winfrey and Williams

7. Frida Kahlo

Frida Kahlo began painting in earnest while recovering from the 1925 bus accident that shattered her spine and pelvis and left her in pain for life. Working from her bed in Coyoacán, Mexico City, she produced a small, fierce body of work, roughly a third of it self-portraits that turned her own body, her Mexican heritage and her suffering into some of the most recognisable images of the twentieth century.

Recognition abroad came late in her short life: a first solo exhibition in New York in 1938 and, in 1939, the French state’s purchase of The Frame, which made her the first twentieth-century Mexican artist in France’s national collection. The Two Fridas, painted the same year, is her best-known canvas. Her fame has only grown since her death in 1954: in November 2025 her 1940 painting The Dream (The Bed) sold at auction for $54.7 million, a record for any work by a woman artist.

  • Born: 6 July 1907, Coyoacán, Mexico City; died 13 July 1954.
  • Field: Painting.
  • Defining achievement: Self-portraits, above all The Two Fridas (1939).
  • Legacy: Her auction record of $54.7 million (2025) confirms her market and cultural standing.

8. Oprah Winfrey

Oprah Winfrey’s influence rests on a simple structural fact: she owned the thing she starred in. Born in rural Mississippi in 1954 and raised in poverty, she became a broadcaster in Nashville and then Chicago, where The Oprah Winfrey Show ran nationally from 1986 to 2011. Through her company Harpo Productions she took ownership of the programme itself, a deal almost no talk-show host, and no Black woman in American television, had achieved.

The show made her a billionaire, widely described as the first Black woman to reach that position, and the platform kept widening: Oprah’s Book Club, launched in 1996, could put a novel on the bestseller lists overnight and still runs today, and in 2011 she launched her own network, OWN. In 2024 she stepped down from the board of Weight Watchers and donated her shares. Philanthropy, including her Leadership Academy for Girls in South Africa, remains a large part of her work.

  • Born: 29 January 1954, Kosciusko, Mississippi.
  • Field: Television, publishing and business.
  • Defining achievement: Building a 25-year talk show into a self-owned media empire.
  • Current role: Chair of Harpo Productions; the Book Club and OWN continue.

9. Serena Williams

Serena Williams learned tennis on public courts in Compton, California, coached by her father Richard alongside her sister Venus, and went on to redefine the women’s game. She won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, more than any other player in the Open era, held the world number one ranking for 319 weeks, and won four Olympic gold medals, one in singles and three in doubles with Venus.

In September 2022, at the US Open, she stepped away from the tour, carefully saying she was “evolving away” rather than retiring, and built a second career through Serena Ventures, whose $111 million inaugural fund backs founders from underrepresented groups; she also became a co-owner of the Toronto Tempo basketball team. Then came the coda few believed: after re-entering the anti-doping testing pool in late 2025, she returned to the court at Queen’s Club in June 2026, playing doubles, four years after her last match.

  • Born: 26 September 1981, Saginaw, Michigan.
  • Field: Tennis, then venture capital and team ownership.
  • Defining achievement: 23 Grand Slam singles titles, an Open era record.
  • Current role: Founder of Serena Ventures; returned to competition in 2026.

Heads of Government and Public Leadership

10. Indira Gandhi

Indira Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru’s daughter, became prime minister in 1966 and dominated Indian politics for most of two decades: in office from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her death. She remains India’s first and only woman prime minister, and its second-longest-serving. Her defining triumph was the 1971 war, in which India’s victory over Pakistan midwifed the new nation of Bangladesh.

Her record also carries the darkest chapter in modern Indian democracy. In June 1975, facing a court ruling against her election, she declared a state of Emergency: for 21 months civil liberties were suspended, the press was censored and opponents jailed. Voters threw her out in 1977, then returned her in 1980. In June 1984 she ordered the army into the Golden Temple at Amritsar; on 31 October 1984 two of her own Sikh bodyguards assassinated her in revenge.

  • Born: 19 November 1917, Allahabad; died 31 October 1984, New Delhi.
  • Field: Politics.
  • Defining achievement: Prime Minister of India for fifteen years across four terms.
  • Legacy: Both the 1971 victory and the Emergency define her contested place in history.

11. Angela Merkel

Angela Merkel grew up in East Germany and trained as a physicist, completing a doctorate in quantum chemistry before entering politics as communism collapsed. She rose through the Christian Democratic Union and in 2005 became Germany’s first woman chancellor. She held the office for sixteen years, winning four elections, and became the central crisis manager of her era: the eurozone debt crisis, the 2015 migration crisis and the first years of the pandemic all ran through her chancellery.

She left office in 2021 on her own timetable, a rarity among long-serving leaders, and has kept the low profile she promised. Her memoir Freedom: Memories 1954–2021, published in November 2024 and written with her longtime aide Beate Baumann, became an international bestseller and a rare frank account of her years in power. In 2026 she remains out of office, appearing mainly for the book’s international launches and public conversations, and has dismissed any return, calling talk of a federal presidency “absurd”.

  • Born: 17 July 1954, Hamburg, West Germany.
  • Field: Politics.
  • Defining achievement: Sixteen years as Chancellor of Germany (2005–2021).
  • Current position: Retired from office; author of the memoir Freedom (2024).

12. Ursula von der Leyen

Ursula von der Leyen, a doctor by training, spent fourteen years in Angela Merkel’s cabinets, including six as Germany’s first woman defence minister, before moving to Brussels. In December 2019 she became President of the European Commission, the European Union’s executive, and the first woman to hold the post. Her first term delivered the European Green Deal and steered the EU’s joint purchase of COVID-19 vaccines.

The European Parliament re-elected her in July 2024 with 401 votes, and her second term, running to 2029, began that December. Its agenda has shifted with the times: competitiveness and cutting red tape, a Clean Industrial Deal, and a new emphasis on European defence, including the Readiness 2030 programme, alongside continued support for Ukraine. She is, by common consent, the most powerful woman in world politics today.

  • Born: 8 October 1958, Brussels, Belgium.
  • Field: Politics.
  • Defining achievement: First woman to lead the European Commission.
  • Current role: Commission President in her second term (2024–2029).

13. Kamala Harris

Kamala Harris climbed every rung of American public law: district attorney of San Francisco, attorney general of California, United States senator. In January 2021 she was sworn in as Vice President, the first woman, the first Black American and the first person of South Asian descent to hold the office. Her four years in the White House made her the most senior woman in American political history.

When President Biden withdrew from the 2024 election, Harris became the Democratic nominee and ran a campaign of just 107 days, losing to Donald Trump in November. She left office in January 2025 and the following July ruled out running for governor of California. Her memoir 107 Days appeared in September 2025. Through 2026 she has campaigned for Democrats ahead of the midterm elections and, asked about another presidential run in 2028, says she has not decided.

  • Born: 20 October 1964, Oakland, California.
  • Field: Law and politics.
  • Defining achievement: First woman Vice President of the United States.
  • Current position: Former vice president; undecided on a 2028 run, by her own account.

14. Jacinda Ardern

Jacinda Ardern became prime minister of New Zealand in October 2017 at thirty-seven, the country’s youngest leader in more than 150 years and, at that moment, the world’s youngest female head of government. In 2018 she became only the second elected head of government in history to give birth in office. Her response to the Christchurch mosque shootings of March 2019, embracing the Muslim community and reforming gun laws within weeks, defined her international reputation.

Her government’s elimination strategy kept New Zealand’s COVID-19 deaths among the lowest in the world, though the long border closure divided opinion at home. In January 2023 she resigned, saying she no longer had “enough in the tank”. Since then she has taken up fellowships at Harvard, founded the Field Fellowship for empathetic leadership, joined the board of the Earthshot Prize, and published a bestselling memoir, A Different Kind of Power, in June 2025.

  • Born: 26 July 1980, Hamilton, New Zealand.
  • Field: Politics.
  • Defining achievement: Prime Minister of New Zealand (2017–2023), elected at 37.
  • Current role: Harvard fellow; founder of the Field Fellowship; memoirist.

15. Nirmala Sitharaman

Nirmala Sitharaman became India’s first full-time woman finance minister in May 2019, having already served as defence minister, only the second woman to hold that post. The finance job made her the custodian of the world’s fifth-largest economy through its hardest years: the pandemic, the inflation that followed, and the push to make India the fastest-growing major economy.

Budget day has become her signature. On 1 February 2026 she presented her ninth consecutive Union Budget, a record for an Indian finance minister: no one before her had presented nine in a row, and she is now the longest-serving finance minister in continuous office. She also holds the record for the longest Budget speech, two hours and forty minutes in 2020. She remains in post through 2026, at the centre of the economic policy of the Modi government’s third term.

  • Born: 18 August 1959, Madurai, Tamil Nadu.
  • Field: Politics and public finance.
  • Defining achievement: A record nine consecutive Union Budgets (2019–2026).
  • Current role: Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs of India.

The Patterns Across Their Lives

Fifteen unlike careers still rhyme. Read together, the same few patterns keep appearing, and they say as much about the world these women entered as about the women themselves.

  • They were first, and usually alone. First woman to a Nobel science prize, to a solo Atlantic crossing, to the chancellery, to the vice presidency, to a ninth straight Budget. Almost every woman here opened a door that had never been opened by a woman before.
  • Institutions outlived them. The Missionaries of Charity, the Jane Goodall Institute, the Malala Fund, the Ninety-Nines and Serena Ventures all still operate. Influence that is built into an organisation survives its founder.
  • The price was real. Curie’s radiation, Parks’s arrest and lost livelihood, Malala’s bullet, Gandhi’s assassination, Earhart’s disappearance. None of these stories is a simple rise.
  • Several reinvented themselves. Merkel the physicist became a chancellor; Williams the champion became an investor, then a player again; Ardern turned a premiership into a study of leadership itself.
  • Second acts are now part of the record. Memoirs by Merkel, Ardern, Harris and Malala in 2024 and 2025 have let four of them reframe their own stories in their own words.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the most influential woman in the world today?

By the measure of formal power, Ursula von der Leyen, who leads the executive of the European Union in a second term to 2029. By the measure of cultural reach, the answer is harder: Oprah Winfrey still shapes what millions read and watch, and Malala Yousafzai remains the global voice for girls’ education. Influence has no single table, which is why this list explains records rather than awarding a single crown.

Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?

Marie Curie. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and won the Chemistry prize outright in 1911. She is still the only person, of any sex, to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Who is the youngest Nobel laureate ever?

Malala Yousafzai, who was seventeen when she received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014. She had survived an assassination attempt two years earlier and co-founded the Malala Fund while still at school.

How many of the fifteen are still living?

Eight. Angela Merkel, Oprah Winfrey, Serena Williams, Ursula von der Leyen, Kamala Harris, Jacinda Ardern, Malala Yousafzai and Nirmala Sitharaman are all living, and von der Leyen and Sitharaman remain in office. Jane Goodall, the most recent loss, died in October 2025 at the age of 91.

Why are the women grouped rather than ranked 1 to 15?

Because the achievements are not commensurable: there is no honest scale on which a Nobel Prize in Physics outweighs a bus boycott, or a Grand Slam title a term as chancellor. Grouping by field, with the record stated plainly for each woman, lets readers make their own comparisons on real evidence.

Sources and Photograph Credits

Biographical details and current positions were researched in November 2026 from the reference and institutional sources listed in the pack’s sources file, including Encyclopaedia Britannica, the Nobel Prize organisation, the Jane Goodall Institute, the European Parliament’s research service and India’s Press Information Bureau reporting. Photographs are real photographs of each woman from Wikimedia Commons, identity-checked against the file records:

  • Photograph: Marie Curie (Henri Manuel, public domain).
  • Photograph: Amelia Earhart (Smithsonian Institution, public domain).
  • Photograph: Rosa Parks (Gene Herrick for the Associated Press, 1956, public domain).
  • Photograph: Frida Kahlo (Guillermo Kahlo, 1932, public domain).
  • Photograph: Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India).
  • Photograph: Mother Teresa (Túrelio, 1986, CC BY-SA 2.0 DE).
  • Photograph: Jane Goodall (Franz Johann Morgenbesser, 2015, CC BY-SA 2.0 — cropped from the original award photograph).
  • Photograph: Angela Merkel (Kristof Roomp, 2019, CC0).
  • Photograph: Oprah Winfrey (aphrodite-in-nyc, 2014, CC BY 2.0).
  • Photograph: Serena Williams (Paulobrad, 2012, CC BY-SA 4.0).
  • Photograph: Ursula von der Leyen (Dati Bendo, European Union, 2023, CC BY 4.0 — cropped to the subject from the original press-conference photograph).
  • Photograph: Kamala Harris (Lawrence Jackson, White House, 2021, public domain).
  • Photograph: Jacinda Ardern (Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, New Zealand, 2019, CC BY 4.0).
  • Photograph: Malala Yousafzai (DFID, 2015, CC BY 2.0).
  • Photograph: Nirmala Sitharaman (Ministry of Finance, Government of India, 2023, GODL-India).

The featured cover compiles the photographs of Marie Curie, Rosa Parks, Kamala Harris and Malala Yousafzai. This is an editorial selection, not an official ranking.

Each with a verified photograph, the achievement she is known for, and why it mattered. An editorial selection, not an official ranking.

title.rendered: Sidhu Moose Wala Murder Case: What Happened, What Police Allege, and Where the Case Stands

content.rendered:
Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala, whose real name was Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu, was shot dead on 29 May 2022 near Jawaharke village in Punjab’s Mansa district. He was 28. Two companions travelling with him were injured. The killing happened one day after Punjab Police reduced his security cover, and it remains one of the most closely followed criminal cases in Punjab.

More than four years later, the case has still not produced a verdict. As of 5 November 2026, the trial is at the evidence stage in the District and Sessions Court at Mansa, charges have been framed against 27 accused, and no accused has been convicted. One key accused, Goldy Brar, has never been arrested and was added to the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in September 2026.

How to read this article: this case is unfinished, so the distinctions matter. Statements presented as fact rest on court reporting and the established public record. Statements introduced with “police allege” or “according to the chargesheet” are allegations the prosecution must prove. Statements by accused persons are their own claims. Every accused person is presumed innocent until a court decides otherwise.

Key facts

  • The victim: Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu, known as Sidhu Moose Wala, born 11 June 1993 in Moosa village, Mansa district; killed aged 28 on 29 May 2022.
  • The attack: his vehicle was intercepted near Jawaharke village, Mansa. His companions Gurwinder Singh and Gurpreet Singh were injured; Moose Wala was declared dead at the Civil Hospital, Mansa.
  • The complaint: the FIR was registered on the complaint of his father, Balkaur Singh, who had been following in a second vehicle. A Special Investigation Team led by Anti-Gangster Task Force chief Pramod Ban investigated.
  • The claim: Goldy Brar publicly claimed responsibility within hours. A claim is not proof; no court has tested it, and Moose Wala was never charged in the earlier murder Brar cited as his motive.
  • The allegation: according to the chargesheet, the murder was planned by Brar in coordination with Lawrence Bishnoi, Jaggu Bhagwanpuria and others, and the chargesheet names Bishnoi as the mastermind. All of this remains to be proved at trial.
  • Charges framed: on 1 May 2024 the Mansa sessions court framed charges against 27 accused. No charges have been framed against Brar, who has never been arrested or produced before the court.
  • Trial status, as of 5 November 2026: evidence stage; the prosecution list runs to roughly 180 witnesses; no conviction has been recorded.
  • International angle: India designated Brar a terrorist under the UAPA in January 2024; the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on 28 September 2026, with a reward of up to $1 million.
  • Anmol Bishnoi: named as an absconding accused in this case, he was deported from the United States in November 2025 and is in Tihar Jail in the National Investigation Agency’s separate case. As of 5 November 2026, he has not been produced before the Mansa court in the Moose Wala case.

The singer and his rise

Moose Wala was the only child of Balkaur Singh and Charan Kaur. He studied electrical engineering at Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College in Ludhiana, graduating in 2016, and then moved to Brampton, Canada, as an international student. His route into music ran through other people’s songs first: he began as a lyricist, writing “License” for the singer Ninja.

His own turn as a singer began with “G Wagon”, and the breakthrough came in 2017 with “So High”, produced by Byg Byrd, which won him Best Lyricist at the Brit Asia TV Music Awards. The debut album PBX 1 followed in 2018. By the time of Moosetape in 2021, anchored by the song “295”, he had become one of Punjabi music’s biggest global names.

He also moved into films, acting in Punjabi productions including Moosa Jatt, and into politics. In the 2022 Punjab Assembly election he stood as the Congress candidate from Mansa, his home constituency, and was defeated. “The Last Ride”, one of his final releases, came out in the last weeks of his life.

29 May 2022: what happened

On 28 May 2022, Punjab Police scaled back the security cover of protectees across the state. Reporting of the chargesheet records that Moose Wala’s own detail was cut from four personnel to two. The timing of that reduction, one day before the killing, has remained one of the case’s most contested background facts.

On the afternoon of 29 May, Moose Wala was travelling in his vehicle near Jawaharke village with Gurwinder Singh and Gurpreet Singh when the vehicle was intercepted and fired on. Both companions were injured. According to the FIR, registered on Balkaur Singh’s complaint, his father was following in a second vehicle with the remaining security personnel and reached the scene shortly afterwards.

Moose Wala was taken to the Civil Hospital in Mansa, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem findings reported at the time recorded multiple gunshot injuries. Beyond that single line, this article does not dwell on the mechanics of the shooting; what matters legally is what the prosecution can prove about who planned and carried it out.

The claim of responsibility

Within hours of the killing, Goldy Brar claimed responsibility in a social-media post. He presented the murder as revenge for the August 2021 killing of Youth Akali Dal leader Vicky Middukhera. That framing is Brar’s own account of motive. It is not a court finding, and it is important to record that Moose Wala was never charged in the Middukhera case and no court has found him connected to it.

Brar repeated the claim in 2025, in an audio interview for the BBC World Service documentary The Killing Call, again saying he had ordered the killing. Moose Wala’s family objected to the documentary, and Balkaur Singh petitioned a Mansa court to stop its screening, arguing it was made without the family’s consent while the trial was under way. The BBC released it on YouTube in June 2025 ahead of the planned screening.

The investigation

Punjab Police set up a Special Investigation Team headed by Pramod Ban, the chief of the Anti-Gangster Task Force. Police say their investigation identified six shooters, working in two groups, and a wider circle of people accused of planning, financing, sheltering or supplying the attack. Those identifications are the prosecution’s case, to be tested against the evidence at trial.

The first arrests of alleged shooters came within weeks. Delhi Police’s Special Cell arrested Priyavrat Fauji and Kashish, also known as Kuldeep, in June 2022, and Ankit Sirsa in early July. Sachin Bhiwani, accused of providing support to the group, was also arrested in that phase of the investigation.

Two of the six men police identified as shooters, Jagroop Singh Roopa and Manpreet Singh “Mannu” Kussa, were killed on 20 July 2022 in an encounter with Punjab Police near Bhakna village in Amritsar district. Police said an AK-47 and a pistol were recovered from the spot. Because both men died before any trial, their alleged roles will never be tested in court in the usual way.

The sixth identified shooter, Deepak Mundi, was arrested on 10 September 2022 near the West Bengal–Nepal border, along with Kapil Pandit and Rajinder, whom police accuse of providing logistics and weapons. Another accused, Sachin Thapan, had left India; police say he travelled on a forged passport. He was detained in Azerbaijan and brought back to India, reported in January 2023.

The investigation produced a series of chargesheets rather than a single document. Hindustan Times court reporting records that the SIT ultimately filed five chargesheets — one main chargesheet and supplementary filings — against 32 accused in total. The FIR itself had booked 36 people, so the numbers in this case differ at each stage: booked, chargesheeted and charged are three different things.

Who has been charged

The first chargesheet was filed on 26 August 2022. Contemporary reporting describes a document of 1,850 pages naming 24 accused and 122 witnesses. Four of the 24 were named as absconding abroad: Goldy Brar, Sachin Thapan, Anmol Bishnoi and Lipin Nehra.

The decisive procedural step came almost two years later. On 1 May 2024, District and Sessions Judge Hari Singh Grewal framed charges against 27 accused, including Lawrence Bishnoi and Jaggu Bhagwanpuria. Framing charges means the court found a prima facie case to answer; it is not a finding of guilt. The same order dismissed the discharge applications of Bishnoi, Bhagwanpuria, Jagtar Singh and Charanjit Singh Chetan.

  • Principal charges framed: Indian Penal Code sections 302 (murder), 307 (attempt to murder), 326 (voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons), 148 (rioting, armed with a deadly weapon), 201 (causing disappearance of evidence), 212 (harbouring an offender) and 120-B (criminal conspiracy), together with offences under the Arms Act.
  • The prosecution’s core allegation: according to the chargesheet, the killing was planned by Brar in coordination with Bishnoi, Bhagwanpuria and others; the chargesheet names Bishnoi as the mastermind.
  • Not charged by the court: Goldy Brar. Charges can only be framed against an accused who has been arrested and produced, and Brar has never been in custody in this case.

Lawrence Bishnoi’s position follows from that. He is an accused in this case, facing framed charges, and the “mastermind” description is the chargesheet’s allegation, not a verdict. He remains in custody in Sabarmati Central Jail, Ahmedabad. A Union Home Ministry order, first issued in August 2023 under section 268 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and continued under section 303 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, bars his removal from that jail while it is in force and has been renewed annually; investigators may question him inside the jail with court permission, and court proceedings use video conferencing where permitted.

Anmol Bishnoi, Lawrence Bishnoi’s younger brother, occupies a different position again, and his cases must not be merged. In the Moose Wala case he is named as an accused who absconded. Separately, the National Investigation Agency chargesheeted him in March 2023 in its own case concerning an alleged terror-gangster syndicate. It was in that NIA case that he was arrested when he was deported from the United States in November 2025, as the next sections explain.

The trial’s current stage

Status as of 5 November 2026: the trial is at the evidence stage before the District and Sessions Court, Mansa. The prosecution is still presenting its witnesses. No accused has been convicted, and no verdict is close, because the witness list is long and progress through it has been slow.

The scale of the task explains much of the delay. The prosecution list runs to roughly 180 witnesses. At a bail hearing in September 2026, the defence pointed out that only 20 of them had been examined by then. The Punjab and Haryana High Court dismissed the bail plea of Joginder Singh, known as Joga, on 4 September 2026; the order described him, on the allegations before it, as “one of the prime conspirators”. A bail order decides custody, not guilt, and that description remains an allegation.

The complainant is also the case’s central witness. Balkaur Singh identified six accused in court, including four alleged shooters — Deepak Mundi, Priyavrat Fauji, Ankit Sirsa and Kuldeep Kashish — and the two vehicles used in the attack. His testimony was recorded in part and his cross-examination has continued across later hearings, a pattern visible through 2026: a witness partly examined in January, the hearing adjourned to 6 February, and six prosecution witnesses examined at a single hearing in April.

Bail decisions during the trial cut both ways, and neither kind is a verdict. In March 2026 the Supreme Court granted bail to Pawan Bishnoi and Jagtar Singh after more than three and a half years in custody, in arguments centred on delay and the number of witnesses still to be heard. The prosecution told the court that protected witnesses had already testified. Bail leaves both men facing the trial as accused; it is not an acquittal.

One procedural thread remains unresolved. Anmol Bishnoi’s counsel filed a plea in February 2026 asking the Mansa court to issue a production warrant so that he could be brought from Tihar Jail and taken into custody in this case. The State filed its reply in September 2026, and the court fixed 9 October 2026 for arguments on the plea. Reporting available as of 5 November 2026 does not record his production before the Mansa court.

The international angle: Goldy Brar

Satinderjeet Singh, known as Goldy Brar, is the accused the Indian case cannot reach. Police allege that he planned the murder in coordination with Lawrence Bishnoi and others, and he has publicly claimed responsibility twice. In January 2024 India designated him a terrorist under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. He has never been arrested in the Moose Wala case, never been produced before the Mansa court, and no Indian court has framed charges against him.

His position changed sharply in 2026 — in the United States, not in India. On 28 September 2026 the FBI added Brar to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, as the list’s 543rd addition, and offered a reward of up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest.

The American case behind the listing is separate from the Mansa trial. A federal arrest warrant was issued on 1 July 2026 in the Central District of California. The FBI says Brar is charged there with RICO conspiracy, conspiracy to interfere with commerce by extortion and attempted interference, and conspiracy to distribute and possess controlled substances. The FBI alleges his involvement in what it calls the Lawrence Bishnoi Organized Crime Group. Those are United States allegations, unproven in any court.

Two consequences follow, and both should be stated plainly. The FBI listing is not an Indian conviction, and it does not move the Mansa trial forward by itself. But it does mean the man the chargesheet places at the centre of the alleged plan is now the subject of an active, public, international hunt, while the trial of those who are in custody proceeds without him.

Anmol Bishnoi’s return shows the other side of the international picture: an accused can be brought to India and still remain out of a particular trial’s reach. Deported from the United States on 18–19 November 2025, he was arrested on arrival by the NIA in its separate 2022 syndicate case and lodged in Tihar Jail. A Home Ministry order dated 5 December 2025, under section 303 of the BNSS, restricts his removal from Tihar for a year or until the relevant trial completes. The practical effect, as The Print reported, is that the Punjab SIT has not secured his physical custody in the Moose Wala case, even though Anmol himself has sought production before the Mansa court.

The family’s campaign

The case has a complainant who has never stepped back from it. Balkaur Singh registered the FIR, attends the Mansa trial as a principal witness, and has pressed throughout for regular hearings and a speedy outcome. His evidence, described above, is itself part of the trial record, which makes his dual role — grieving father and prosecution witness — unusual in its visibility.

His campaign has also been public. In 2023 he sat in protest outside the Punjab Assembly over the pace of the investigation. Earlier, in December 2022, he had publicly offered a reward of ₹2 crore from his own pocket for information leading to Brar’s arrest, a measure of how central the fugitive’s absence has been to the family’s sense that justice is incomplete.

Politics has repeatedly tried to claim the family’s cause, and the family has repeatedly set its own terms. In April 2024 Balkaur Singh decided not to contest the Bathinda Lok Sabha seat after meeting Congress leaders; the family’s stated position was that speedy justice in the murder case came first.

The campaign continues alongside the trial. On 20 October 2026, having returned from abroad after the postponement of remaining hologram-tour shows, he visited a protest in Mansa over the killing of anti-drug activist Parvinder Jhota and urged that the gangster issue be raised with the Union Home Minister.

His most recent intervention came on 4 November 2026. After a former AAP legislator alleged that an AAP leader had publicised the withdrawal of Moose Wala’s security cover, Balkaur Singh sought an impartial investigation into the allegation. His stated point was that his son’s murder should not be reduced to political rhetoric — a position consistent with the family’s approach throughout: every aspect of the case, investigated properly, and decided in court.

Legacy

Moose Wala’s music did not stop with his death; in part, it was only beginning its public life. “SYL”, released posthumously on 23 June 2022, became one of his most discussed songs before it was blocked in India following a legal complaint. His family and team have continued to release recordings he made before his death, keeping the catalogue active rather than treating it as closed.

That process is still under way. PTC News reported on 16 October 2026 that “Kaali Hoodie”, featuring Bohemia and released after the Vancouver show of the hologram tour, was his 14th posthumous song, following the 13th, “Ghostface Killah”, the previous month. Song counts of this kind are reported figures, and they will keep changing while unreleased recordings remain.

The most striking development is the Signed to God hologram world tour, backed by his family, which opened at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena on 9 October 2026, a day later than first scheduled. The production pairs his original vocals with a physical performance model built in Italy using a body double and prosthetics. Reporting of the family’s position says the show deliberately avoids AI-generated songs or an invented new persona, and that Moose Wala had himself discussed performing for audiences without physically travelling.

The legacy and the case now run in parallel, and each shapes the other. A hologram tour can extend a singer’s presence indefinitely; it cannot answer the question the Mansa court exists to decide. Until that court delivers a verdict, the honest summary stands: the identified shooters have been arrested or are dead, the alleged organisers are in custody in India or sought abroad, charges are framed and evidence is being recorded — and responsibility for the murder of Sidhu Moose Wala has still not been determined by any court.

Timeline

  • 11 June 1993: Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu is born in Moosa village, Mansa district, Punjab.
  • 2016: graduates in electrical engineering from Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College, Ludhiana, and moves to Canada as an international student.
  • 2017: breakthrough with “So High”; Best Lyricist at the Brit Asia TV Music Awards.
  • 2018: debut album PBX 1 released.
  • 2021: Moosetape released, including “295”; acts in Moosa Jatt.
  • Early 2022: contests the Punjab Assembly election from Mansa as a Congress candidate and is defeated.
  • 28 May 2022: Punjab Police scale back security cover; reporting of the chargesheet puts Moose Wala’s detail at two personnel, down from four.
  • 29 May 2022: Moose Wala is shot dead near Jawaharke village, Mansa. The FIR is registered on his father’s complaint; Brar claims responsibility within hours.
  • June–July 2022: Delhi Police Special Cell arrests alleged shooters Priyavrat Fauji, Kashish and Ankit Sirsa; Sachin Bhiwani is also arrested.
  • 20 July 2022: identified shooters Jagroop Singh Roopa and Manpreet Singh “Mannu” Kussa are killed in a police encounter near Bhakna village, Amritsar district.
  • 26 August 2022: first chargesheet filed: 1,850 pages, 24 accused, 122 witnesses.
  • 10 September 2022: Deepak Mundi, the sixth identified shooter, is arrested near the West Bengal–Nepal border.
  • December 2022: Balkaur Singh publicly offers ₹2 crore from his own pocket for information leading to Brar’s arrest.
  • January 2023: Sachin Thapan, whom police say fled on a forged passport, is brought back to India from Azerbaijan.
  • March 2023: the NIA chargesheets Anmol Bishnoi in its separate alleged terror-gangster syndicate case.
  • January 2024: India designates Goldy Brar a terrorist under the UAPA.
  • 1 May 2024: the Mansa sessions court frames charges against 27 accused, including Lawrence Bishnoi and Jaggu Bhagwanpuria.
  • June 2025: the BBC releases The Killing Call; Brar repeats his claim of responsibility in it; the family’s petition against the screening is before a Mansa court.
  • 18–19 November 2025: Anmol Bishnoi is deported from the United States and arrested on arrival by the NIA in its separate case; he is lodged in Tihar Jail.
  • 5 December 2025: a Home Ministry order under BNSS section 303 restricts Anmol Bishnoi’s removal from Tihar Jail.
  • March 2026: the Supreme Court grants bail to accused Pawan Bishnoi and Jagtar Singh after more than three and a half years in custody.
  • 4 September 2026: the Punjab and Haryana High Court dismisses Joginder Singh “Joga”’s bail plea; the hearing records that only 20 of roughly 180 prosecution witnesses have been examined.
  • 28 September 2026: the FBI adds Goldy Brar to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, with a reward of up to $1 million.
  • 9 October 2026: the Signed to God hologram tour opens in Toronto; the same day is fixed for arguments in Mansa on Anmol Bishnoi’s production plea.
  • 4 November 2026: Balkaur Singh seeks an impartial investigation into allegations about the publicising of his son’s security withdrawal.
  • 5 November 2026: status checked for this article: trial at the evidence stage in Mansa; no convictions.

Frequently asked questions

Who was Sidhu Moose Wala?

Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu (1993–2022) was a Punjabi singer, songwriter and actor from Moosa village in Mansa district. He rose from writing songs for other artists to global success with tracks such as “So High” and “295”, acted in Punjabi films, and contested the 2022 Punjab Assembly election from Mansa as a Congress candidate.

What happened on 29 May 2022?

Moose Wala was travelling near Jawaharke village in Mansa district with two companions when his vehicle was intercepted and fired on. His companions were injured; he was declared dead at the Civil Hospital, Mansa. The attack came a day after his police security cover had been reduced. His father, following in a second vehicle, became the FIR’s complainant.

Has anyone been convicted of the murder?

No. As of 5 November 2026, the trial is at the evidence stage in the District and Sessions Court, Mansa. Charges were framed against 27 accused on 1 May 2024, but framing charges is not a conviction. Two of the six men police identified as shooters died in a police encounter in July 2022, before any trial.

What roles do police allege Lawrence Bishnoi, Goldy Brar and Anmol Bishnoi played?

According to the chargesheet, the murder was planned by Brar in coordination with Bishnoi, Jaggu Bhagwanpuria and others, and Bishnoi is named as the mastermind. Anmol Bishnoi, Lawrence’s younger brother, is named as an accused who absconded. These are allegations the prosecution must prove; none of the three has been convicted in this case.

Why have no charges been framed against Goldy Brar?

Because he has never been arrested in this case. An Indian court frames charges against an accused who is produced before it. Brar remains abroad and at large. India designated him a terrorist under the UAPA in January 2024, and on 28 September 2026 the FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in connection with a separate United States federal case.

Did Goldy Brar admit to the killing?

He has claimed responsibility, first in a social-media post within hours of the murder and again in the BBC documentary The Killing Call in 2025. A public claim is not evidence tested in court, and it is not an admission recorded before a judge. Brar’s stated motive was revenge for the 2021 murder of Vicky Middukhera; Moose Wala was never charged in that case.

What happens next in the trial?

The prosecution continues to present its witnesses — roughly 180 are listed, and only a fraction had been examined by September 2026, so the evidence stage is likely to run for some time. Alongside it, the Mansa court is dealing with Anmol Bishnoi’s plea for production from Tihar Jail, and Brar’s capture remains a matter for international agencies. No verdict date can responsibly be predicted.

Research note: this article was researched and written afresh on 5 November 2026 from reputable published reporting, principally The Indian Express, The Tribune, Hindustan Times, The Print and the FBI’s own publications, with case status checked as of 5 November 2026. Allegations are attributed throughout and remain subject to the court’s verdict.

excerpt.rendered: Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala was shot dead near Jawaharke village in Punjab’s Mansa district on 29 May 2022, a day after his security cover was reduced. Goldy Brar claimed responsibility; Punjab Police allege Lawrence Bishnoi masterminded the killing. A factual explainer: what happened, what is alleged, and where the trial stands as of October 2026.

title.rendered: Top 13 Jewellers in India: Leading Jewellery Brands Profiled (2026)

content.rendered:
India buys more gold jewellery than any other country, and the way people buy it has changed. Family-run single shops still matter, but a growing share of purchases now happens at organised chains that sell only hallmarked jewellery, publish their buyback terms and run stores across many states. Knowing how these big jewellers differ helps you pay the right making charges and choose a store whose policies suit you.

This guide profiles the 13 jewellers that shape the national market in November 2026, from a Mumbai house trading since 1864 to a Reliance Retail brand launched in 2007. Each profile uses freshly checked facts, including store counts as of late 2026 where a company has published them. A buying guide and answers to common questions follow the profiles.

The shift towards organised chains has practical benefits for buyers: hallmarked-only stock, printed price breakup on the bill and written exchange policies. The trade-off is that making charges and buyback deductions vary a lot between chains, so the jeweller you choose affects what the same gold costs you over its lifetime.

Quick answer

  • Largest network: Tanishq, with 505 stores in India as of March 2025, plus stores overseas.
  • Widest global reach: Malabar Gold and Diamonds, with more than 400 showrooms across 14 countries.
  • Oldest name: TBZ, The Original, trading in Mumbai since 1864.
  • Strongest in the South: GRT Jewellers, Jos Alukkas and Bhima Jewellers, all rooted in Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
  • Strongest in the East: Senco Gold and Diamonds, based in Kolkata since 1938.
  • Traditional Maharashtrian designs: WHP Jewellers of Mumbai, founded in 1909.
  • Comeback story: PC Jeweller, which cleared its bank debt in October 2026 and is expanding again.

Quick comparison

JewellerBased inKnown for
Tanishq (Titan Company)BengaluruIndia's largest jewellery network; Rivaah wedding range
Kalyan JewellersThrissur, KeralaCollections matched to local tastes; Candere online brand
Malabar Gold & DiamondsKozhikode, KeralaGlobal network; published pricing and buyback promises
JoyalukkasThrissur, KeralaCompany-owned stores across India and the Gulf

Senco Gold & DiamondsKolkataEastern India's leading chain; lightweight Everlite range
GRT JewellersChennaiSouth Indian bridal gold; very large flagship stores

Bhima JewellersAlappuzha, KeralaCentury-old family jeweller, strong in Kerala

WHP JewellersMumbaiTraditional Maharashtrian jewellery since 1909
Reliance JewelsMumbai (Reliance Retail)Reliance backing; reach into smaller towns

The 13 jewellers in detail

1. Tanishq (Titan Company)

Tanishq is the jewellery division of Titan Company, part of the Tata group, and the largest jewellery retailer in India by store network. Titan reported 505 Tanishq stores in India as of March 2025, spread across more than 300 cities, with a further set of stores in the UAE, the United States, Qatar and Singapore. The brand began in 1996 and helped make transparent, fixed pricing normal in a market once dominated by bargaining.

Wedding buyers are served by the Rivaah range, while Mia by Tanishq covers lightweight everyday pieces. Stores offer a Karatmeter purity check, and old-gold exchange brings in a large share of sales, with the company putting exchange at roughly 40 per cent of its jewellery business. Tanishq also runs Golden Harvest, the best known of the jewellers' monthly savings schemes, described in the guide below.

Later trade reports during 2025 and 2026 put the India network higher still, at around 540 outlets, as openings continued. At group level, Titan also agreed in 2026 to acquire a 67 per cent stake in the Gulf business of Dubai-based Damas Jewellery, underlining how Indian chains are now expanding abroad as well as at home.

  • Parent company: Titan Company (Tata group), Bengaluru
  • Stores: 505 in India as of March 2025, plus overseas stores
  • Known for: Rivaah bridal range, Mia lightweight range, Karatmeter purity checks
  • Savings scheme: Golden Harvest monthly plan
  • Founded: 1996, as Titan Company's jewellery venture
  • Best for: Pan-India wedding buying with standardised pricing

2. Kalyan Jewellers

Kalyan Jewellers was founded in 1993 in Thrissur, Kerala, by T. S. Kalyanaraman, and grew by matching each store's stock to local tastes rather than selling one national range everywhere. The company's quarterly update reported 469 showrooms as of 31 December 2025: 318 Kalyan stores in India, 38 in the Middle East, two in the United States, one in the United Kingdom and 110 stores of its Candere brand.

Bridal buying is organised around regional wedding lines such as Muhurta, supported by ranges for festivals and daily wear. Candere, its online-first brand, sells lighter, lower-priced jewellery aimed at younger buyers. Kalyan continues to open stores in India and overseas, and market summaries of its June 2026 update put the network at 524 showrooms by 30 June 2026, with Candere alone rising to 129 stores.

  • Founded: 1993, Thrissur, by T. S. Kalyanaraman
  • Stores: 469 showrooms as of 31 December 2025 (company update)
  • Known for: Hyperlocal collections, Muhurta bridal range
  • Also runs: Candere, an online-first lightweight jewellery brand
  • Head office: Thrissur, Kerala
  • Best for: Wedding styles matched to your region's customs

3. Malabar Gold & Diamonds

Malabar Gold and Diamonds was founded in 1993 in Kozhikode, Kerala, by M. P. Ahammed, and has grown into one of the world's largest jewellery retail groups. The company opened its 400th showroom in Noida in June 2025 and reported about 416 showrooms across 14 countries by December 2025, including a first entry into New Zealand. Malabar describes itself as the world's fifth largest jewellery retailer.

The group sells under a set of published customer commitments, the Malabar Promise, covering transparent pricing, buyback terms and lifetime maintenance. It was also among the chains that campaigned for a single gold rate across India. Stores cover heavy South Indian bridal sets as well as diamond, platinum and lightweight ranges, and the Gulf remains a major market alongside India. At the 400-store announcement the group reported turnover of ₹63,000 crore.

  • Founded: 1993, Kozhikode, by M. P. Ahammed
  • Stores: About 416 showrooms in 14 countries as of December 2025
  • Known for: Malabar Promise on pricing, buyback and maintenance
  • Milestone: 400th showroom opened in June 2025
  • Turnover: ₹63,000 crore reported at the 400-store announcement
  • Best for: Families buying across India and the Gulf

4. Joyalukkas

Joyalukkas grew out of a family jewellery business started in Thrissur in 1956. Joy Alukkas took the brand overseas in 1987, opening in the Gulf, and built a chain that now runs more than 190 showrooms across 11 or more countries. Every store is company-owned rather than franchised. India is the largest market, with 109 showrooms in the 2025 financial year and further openings since.

In December 2025 the group announced a ₹3,600 crore plan to open 40 more showrooms, taking the network towards 230 stores. Large-format showrooms carry temple, bridal, diamond and Italian-style collections under ranges such as Veda, Pride and Eleganza. Trade coverage counted 116 Joyalukkas showrooms in India as of March 2026. Like most big South Indian chains, Joyalukkas also runs a monthly gold purchase plan for wedding savers.

  • Roots: Family business from 1956, Thrissur; Gulf expansion from 1987
  • Stores: More than 190 showrooms, all company-owned
  • Known for: Large-format stores, Veda temple and Pride diamond ranges
  • Expansion: ₹3,600 crore plan for 40 new showrooms announced in December 2025
  • India network: 116 showrooms as of March 2026 (trade coverage)
  • Best for: One-stop large-format wedding shopping

5. Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri (TBZ, The Original)

TBZ is the oldest jeweller on this list. The house was founded in 1864 in Zaveri Bazaar, Mumbai, then the centre of India's bullion trade, and still trades from that neighbourhood. The company runs 37 showrooms across India and credits itself with two firsts in its own history: offering a buyback guarantee as early as 1938 and moving early on hallmarked jewellery.

The brand entered a new chapter in 2026. GRT Jewellers signed a share purchase agreement to acquire a 74.12 per cent stake in TBZ for ₹1,033.71 crore, with an open offer to other shareholders planned, according to reports published in August and September 2026. As of November 2026 the transaction was still being completed. TBZ stores continue to trade on their heritage positioning, with Mumbai wedding and diamond jewellery at the core of the range.

  • Founded: 1864, Zaveri Bazaar, Mumbai
  • Stores: 37 showrooms across India
  • Known for: Heritage Mumbai house; wedding and diamond jewellery
  • 2026 update: GRT Jewellers agreed to buy a 74.12 per cent stake for ₹1,033.71 crore
  • Leadership: Chairman and managing director Shrikant Zaveri
  • Best for: Heritage Mumbai designs and diamond jewellery

6. Senco Gold & Diamonds

Senco is Kolkata's best known jewellery house. The Sen family's jewellery business dates to 1938, the modern company was incorporated in 1994, and Senco listed on the stock exchanges in 2023. Its company factsheet counted 186 showrooms as of 30 June 2025, with growth led by franchise stores. The network is strongest in West Bengal and the East and has been pushing into northern markets.

Alongside traditional Bengali gold work, Senco sells the lightweight Everlite range and the fashion-led Sennes brand, and in 2026 it opened dedicated stores for lab-grown diamonds. Trade coverage put the network at about 215 showrooms by September 2026, including Sennes stores and a presence in Dubai. Management has guided for about 20 additional showrooms in the 2027 financial year. For buyers in the East, Senco is usually the organised chain with the deepest local presence.

  • Roots: Family business from 1938, Kolkata; incorporated 1994; listed 2023
  • Stores: 186 showrooms as of 30 June 2025 (company factsheet)
  • Known for: Bengali gold designs, Everlite lightweight range, Sennes fashion brand
  • Recent move: Dedicated lab-grown diamond stores launched in 2026
  • Listing: Listed on Indian stock exchanges in 2023
  • Best for: Bengali gold work and lightweight fashion ranges

7. GRT Jewellers

GRT Jewellers was founded in 1964 in Chennai by G. Rajendran and began as G. R. Thanga Maligai, a name older Chennai shoppers still use. The chain now runs 68 stores in India and one in Singapore, concentrated in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka. Its T. Nagar flagship in Chennai is among the largest jewellery showrooms in India.

GRT is a first choice for South Indian bridal gold, temple jewellery and silver articles, and it runs long-standing monthly savings plans for wedding families. In 2026 the privately held group stepped onto the national stage by agreeing to acquire a controlling stake in Mumbai's TBZ, the oldest jeweller on this list, a deal covered in the TBZ profile above.

The TBZ deal matters beyond Chennai. It gives a southern bridal specialist a heritage Mumbai brand and a ready-made presence in western India, and it pairs two of the oldest names in Indian jewellery retail under one owner. Buyers are unlikely to see the TBZ name disappear; heritage is precisely what GRT is paying for.

  • Founded: 1964, Chennai, by G. Rajendran
  • Stores: 68 in India plus one in Singapore
  • Known for: South Indian bridal gold and temple jewellery
  • 2026 update: Agreed to acquire a controlling stake in TBZ
  • Flagship: T. Nagar, Chennai, among India's largest jewellery showrooms
  • Best for: Temple jewellery, bridal gold and silver articles

8. Jos Alukkas

Jos Alukkas traces its start to 1964 in Thrissur, where Alukka Varghese, known as A. V. Jose, opened the family's first jewellery business. His son Jos Alukkas built the modern chain and pioneered the large-format gold supermarket in Kerala, with big stores carrying deep stock under one roof. The group was also among the early adopters of BIS 916 hallmarked gold.

The network has passed 60 showrooms across South India; the group's 66th showroom opened at Tenkasi in Tamil Nadu. In 2025 the group announced a ₹5,500 crore plan to open 100 stores over seven to eight years, reaching beyond its southern base. The next generation of the family now serves as managing directors alongside the chairman. Actor Dulquer Salmaan was announced as brand ambassador in 2025.

  • Founded: 1964, Thrissur, by A. V. Jose (Alukka Varghese)
  • Stores: More than 60 showrooms in South India
  • Known for: Gold supermarket large-format stores
  • Expansion: ₹5,500 crore plan for 100 new stores announced in 2025
  • Leadership: Chairman Jos Alukkas, with the next generation as managing directors
  • Best for: Deep-stock bridal shopping in Kerala and Tamil Nadu

9. Bhima Jewellers

Bhima Jewellers was founded in 1925 in Alappuzha, Kerala, by K. Lakshminarayana Bhattar, remembered as Bhima Bhattar. It is credited with opening Kerala's first ready-made gold jewellery showroom at a time when most ornaments were made to order. The group completed 100 years in 2025, a milestone few Indian jewellers have reached.

Today the Bhima name covers a network of more than 100 showrooms across South India and the UAE, run as family-owned entities that share the brand; published profiles put the group at around 116 showrooms. Stores are known for Kerala bridal sets, traditional kasumalai necklaces and a loyal local customer base built over generations. For many Kerala families, Bhima remains the default jeweller for wedding purchases.

  • Founded: 1925, Alappuzha, by K. Lakshminarayana Bhattar
  • Stores: More than 100 showrooms across South India and the UAE (group-wide)
  • Known for: Kerala bridal jewellery; first ready-made gold showroom in Kerala
  • Milestone: Centenary completed in 2025
  • Network size: Around 116 showrooms in published group profiles
  • Best for: Kerala bridal sets bought on family trust

10. PC Jeweller

PC Jeweller was founded in 2005 in Delhi and built its name on large-format, wedding-focused showrooms in North India. The company ran more than 80 showrooms at its peak before debt problems forced a long restructuring. It operated 52 showrooms across 37 cities as of 31 March 2026, four of them franchised.

The turnaround reached its marker in October 2026, when the company reported that it had become debt-free, following a September 2024 settlement with a 14-bank consortium and a preferential fund raise of ₹2,702.11 crore the previous year. Quarterly profit rose 58 per cent year on year. PC Jeweller now plans up to 100 new large-format stores over the following 12 to 18 months, largely through franchise partners, and has signed skills and franchise partnerships with NSDC and the Uttar Pradesh CM-YUVA programme.

  • Founded: 2005, Delhi
  • Stores: 52 showrooms in 37 cities as of 31 March 2026
  • Known for: Large-format wedding jewellery stores
  • 2026 update: Reported debt-free in October 2026; up to 100 new stores planned
  • Turnaround: Bank settlement in September 2024 and a ₹2,702.11 crore fund raise
  • Best for: North Indian wedding sets in large showrooms

11. Khazana Jewellery

Khazana Jewellery is a Chennai chain founded by Kishore Kumar Jain. The company's own history records that its first professionally managed showroom opened on Cathedral Road, Chennai, on 10 December 1993, and it has since grown across Tamil Nadu and the wider South. The founding family's bullion trading roots in Nellore go back further, to 1976. The company's website lists 39 showrooms, while store locators suggest the network has grown beyond that figure.

Khazana built its following on lightweight designs that keep ticket sizes accessible, alongside full South Indian wedding sets. The company recalls being an early mover on written buyback assurance, issuing photo guarantee cards so customers could verify the exact piece they had bought. It remains a popular mid-market choice in Tamil Nadu cities and towns.

  • Founded: First showroom opened in Chennai in 1993 (company history)
  • Stores: 39 listed on the company website, mostly in South India
  • Known for: Lightweight, value-led designs and wedding sets
  • Founder: Kishore Kumar Jain
  • Earlier roots: Family bullion trading in Nellore from 1976
  • Best for: Lightweight designs at mid-market prices in Tamil Nadu

12. Waman Hari Pethe Jewellers (WHP)

Waman Hari Pethe Jewellers was founded in 1909 in Girgaon, Mumbai, by brothers Waman Hari Pethe and Ganesh Hari Pethe. The family began with pearl work, earning the name Motiwale Pethe, and the business is now run by the fifth generation. It is one of the oldest continuously trading jewellery houses in Maharashtra.

WHP is the specialist on this list for traditional Maharashtrian jewellery, including the thushi and mohanmala necklaces, the Maharashtrian nath nose ring and vajratik pieces worn at weddings and festivals. Its 25th outlet opened at Dadar in 2021, and its Dadar flagship on Ranade Road reopened after renovation in September 2025, inaugurated by brand ambassador Sharvari Wagh. Stores are spread across Maharashtra, Goa and Indore.

  • Founded: 1909, Girgaon, Mumbai, by the Pethe brothers
  • Stores: Across Maharashtra, Goa and Indore
  • Known for: Maharashtrian traditional jewellery, thushi, mohanmala and nath
  • Recent news: Renovated Dadar flagship reopened in September 2025
  • Family: Run by the fifth generation of the Pethe family
  • Best for: Authentic Maharashtrian wedding jewellery

13. Reliance Jewels

Reliance Jewels is the jewellery brand of Reliance Retail and was launched in 2007. Brand releases in December 2025 put the network at more than 145 showrooms across India, alongside its online store. Reliance Retail's wider footprint gives the brand a presence in smaller towns that many jewellery chains reach later.

The range covers gold, diamond and bridal jewellery, with seasonal events such as the Dream Diamond Sale used to draw wedding and festive buyers. The December 2025 edition of that sale ran across its 145-plus stores into January 2026 with a free gold coin offer. For shoppers who value the backing of a large retail group and a store in their own town, Reliance Jewels is often the most accessible organised option on this list.

  • Launched: 2007, as part of Reliance Retail
  • Stores: More than 145 showrooms as of December 2025 (brand releases)
  • Known for: Reach into smaller towns; gold, diamond and bridal ranges
  • Parent: Reliance Retail, India's largest retailer by network
  • Seasonal event: Dream Diamond Sale, held across its stores
  • Best for: Buyers in smaller towns who want an organised chain nearby

Hallmarking and BIS: check purity before you pay

Every jeweller on this list sells BIS-hallmarked gold. Hallmarking is your main protection against under-caratage, so learn the marks before you visit a store.

  • Hallmarking of gold jewellery has been mandatory in India since June 2021 and now covers 392 districts, according to the Bureau of Indian Standards brief updated in October 2026.
  • A hallmarked piece carries three marks: the BIS logo, the purity and fineness mark such as 22K916, and a six-digit HUID code unique to that piece.
  • Verify the HUID free of charge in the BIS Care app. It shows the jeweller, the assaying centre, the purity and the hallmarking date.
  • Hallmarking covers gold from 9K to 24K. The 9K grade was added in July 2025, bringing budget jewellery into the system.
  • Some items are exempt, including pieces under two grams and kundan, polki and jadau jewellery.
  • For silver, HUID-based hallmarking is available on a voluntary basis from September 2025.
  • Since June 2026, hallmarked pieces also carry a photograph and captured weight in the BIS system, which you can view in the BIS Care app before buying.
  • Older family gold without a HUID can still be exchanged or sold. The jeweller tests its purity, for example with a Karatmeter, and prices it on the result.

Making charges: the part of the bill that varies most

Two jewellers can quote very different prices for similar gold weight because of making charges, the fee for design and labour on top of the metal value. This is where comparison shopping pays.

  • Making charges are quoted as a percentage of the gold value or as a fixed amount per gram, and they rise with the complexity of the design.
  • Plain machine-made pieces sit at the low end. Intricate handcrafted, antique and temple work can cost several times more in making charges.
  • Making charges are never refunded when you sell or exchange a piece. Treat them as the price of the design, not as stored value.
  • Ask for an itemised bill that shows the gold value, making charges, stone charges and tax as separate lines before you pay.
  • GST is charged at 3 per cent on the total transaction value of gold jewellery. The CBIC sectoral guidance confirms the 3 per cent applies whether or not making charges are shown separately.
  • Festive offers usually discount making charges rather than the gold rate. Convert any waiver into rupees on your actual bill before judging it.
  • Compare the same style of piece at two or three jewellers. The gold rate will be similar; the making charge is the real difference.

Which jeweller suits which buyer

  • Kerala or Tamil wedding: Malabar, Jos Alukkas, Bhima, Joyalukkas and GRT carry the deepest traditional bridal stock.
  • Maharashtrian wedding: WHP for thushi, mohanmala and nath; TBZ for Mumbai-style diamond and gold sets.
  • Bengali and eastern styles: Senco, with the widest network in the East.
  • Lightweight daily wear: Mia by Tanishq, Candere by Kalyan and Senco's Everlite keep weights and prices low.
  • Plain gold with low making charges: compare the big South Indian chains and ask each for its lowest-making-charge range in writing.
  • Smaller towns: Reliance Jewels and Kalyan often have the nearest organised store.

Buyback and exchange: read the terms before you buy

Most wedding jewellery is eventually exchanged, so the buyback policy matters as much as the purchase price. Policies differ between chains, and the differences are worth money.

  • On buyback you normally receive the day's gold value for the net weight of your piece at its hallmarked purity. Making charges and GST are not returned.
  • Some policies deduct melting or refining charges. Ask for any deduction in writing before you buy, not when you return.
  • Exchanging at the same jeweller usually gives better value than a cash buyback, and better than selling to a different store.
  • Stones are treated separately. Diamond and gemstone buyback terms vary widely, so check them piece by piece.
  • Keep your invoice and note the HUID of each piece. A verifiable hallmark makes resale or exchange easier at any jeweller.
  • Exchange value and cash buyback value for the same piece can differ on the same day. Ask for both figures before you decide.

Gold schemes: useful, with conditions

Monthly gold schemes help families save towards a wedding, and nearly every chain on this list runs one. Tanishq's Golden Harvest is the best known: you pay a fixed instalment for 11 months and Tanishq adds a bonus at maturity, which you then spend on jewellery.

  • Scheme money can normally be redeemed only as jewellery at that jeweller. Cash refunds and gold coins are usually excluded.
  • The gold price applied is the rate on the day you buy the jewellery, not the rates on the days you paid instalments.
  • These are advance purchase plans run by jewellers, not bank deposits. They carry no deposit insurance and pay no interest in the banking sense.
  • Bonuses usually depend on completing every instalment on time. Missed payments can reduce or cancel the bonus.
  • Choose a scheme only at a jeweller you would happily buy from anyway, because your money is locked to that one store network.
  • Compare the bonus, not the brand. Two plans with the same instalment can offer different bonuses, and some bonuses apply to gold jewellery only, not to diamond pieces or coins.

Before you buy: a short checklist

  • Check the day's gold rate for your city and purity, and confirm the store is applying that rate.
  • Find the BIS logo, the purity mark and the six-digit HUID on the piece, and verify the HUID in the BIS Care app.
  • Ask for the making charge in writing and an itemised bill with gold value, making charges, stone charges and GST on separate lines.
  • Get the buyback and exchange terms, including any melting deduction, before you pay.
  • If you join a gold scheme, read the bonus and missed-instalment conditions on the enrolment form.
  • Keep the invoice, the HUID details and any guarantee cards together; you will need them for exchange, resale or a claim.

How these 13 jewellers were chosen

The list favours jewellers a buyer anywhere in India is likely to meet, from national chains to strong regional houses with decades of trading history.

  • National networks or a dominant presence in at least one major region.
  • Only BIS-hallmarked gold sold, with published buyback or exchange terms.
  • A trading record long enough to judge, or the backing of a large listed group.
  • Coverage across price levels, from lightweight daily wear to heavy bridal sets.
  • Representation from the South, West, East and North, reflecting how Indians actually buy jewellery.

Frequently asked questions

Which is the oldest jeweller on this list?

TBZ, The Original, founded in 1864 in Zaveri Bazaar, Mumbai. WHP Jewellers of Mumbai follows from 1909, and Bhima Jewellers of Alappuzha from 1925. All three still trade under family ownership or family-founded brands today.

What does 22K916 mean on a hallmark?

It means the piece is 22 karat gold with a fineness of 916, that is, 916 parts of pure gold in every 1,000, or 91.6 per cent purity. The rest is alloy added for strength. In the same way, 18K750 means 75 per cent pure gold, the standard for most diamond jewellery.

What is HUID and how do I verify it?

HUID is the six-digit alphanumeric Hallmark Unique Identification code stamped on every hallmarked gold piece since 2021. Download the free BIS Care app, choose Verify HUID, and enter the code. The app shows the jeweller's registration, the assaying centre, the certified purity and the date of hallmarking for that exact piece.

Why do making charges differ so much between jewellers?

Making charges pay for design and labour, so they follow the work involved. A plain machine-made bangle needs little labour, while handcrafted temple or antique jewellery takes skilled days. Brand positioning and store costs also play a part, which is why the same design can carry noticeably different making charges at different chains.

Which jeweller is best for wedding jewellery?

It depends on your tradition and city. Tanishq's Rivaah, Malabar, Joyalukkas, GRT and Jos Alukkas all carry deep bridal ranges, Senco leads in the East, and WHP is the specialist for Maharashtrian weddings. Compare two or three stores on making charges and buyback terms for the weight you plan to buy; that difference usually matters more than the brand.

What tax do I pay when buying gold jewellery?

GST of 3 per cent is charged on the total transaction value of the jewellery. No GST is charged when you later sell gold back to a jeweller. Keep the invoice, because it also records the HUID of each piece and supports any future exchange, buyback or insurance claim.

Store counts and company developments in this guide were checked in November 2026 and are dated where they appear. Jewellery prices move with the daily gold rate, so confirm the rate, making charges and buyback terms in store before you buy.
