title.rendered: Top 20 Dance Academies in Chandigarh for Kids, Beginners and Adults

content.rendered:
Chandigarh has dance academies of very different kinds: a classical examining institution founded in the 1950s, Latin and street-style studios, wedding choreography specialists, and small neighbourhood classes that exist mostly on Instagram. This guide profiles twenty of them in a set order, using each academy's own website or social pages first and reputable directories second.

Every fact below comes from fresh research done for this rewrite. Where an academy's details rest on directories alone, the profile says so; where a listing is marked permanently closed, that is stated rather than hidden, because an out-of-date recommendation helps nobody.

Quick Answer: Best Dance Academies in Chandigarh

  • For classical dance with recognised certification: Pracheen Kala Kendra (Sector 35-B), an examining body teaching Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Manipuri, Odissi and more through graded diplomas.
  • For young children: Pals Dancing Arena (Sector 22-C) publishes dedicated kids' batches for ages 4 to 12 on its own website.
  • For wedding and sangeet choreography: DanceworkZ Studio and The Dance Unity build their offer around it; Pals Dancing Arena and The Dance Mafia also list it.
  • For Salsa, Bachata and Kizomba: Freedom2Dance Studio (Sector 32-D) and Rock N Roll Dance Institute (Sector 35-D).
  • For the widest style list plus fitness: The Dance Mafia (Sector 44-C and Mohali), which adds Zumba and aerobics to a long dance menu.
  • Before you visit any academy: check its official page or call first. A few listings in this guide are marked permanently closed, and each profile flags those cases.

How to Choose a Dance Academy in Chandigarh

  • Decide the goal first: a graded classical diploma, stage performance, fitness, or one wedding routine lead to very different academies.
  • Match the style: classical forms concentrate at Pracheen Kala Kendra; Latin forms at Freedom2Dance and Rock N Roll; street styles at PDA, ShowStoppers and Rockstar Academy.
  • Ask about the batch: age group, level and class size matter more than the academy's name; several academies separate kids, beginners and advanced dancers.
  • Take the trial class: most academies offer one; use it to judge the teacher, the floor and the commute.
  • Verify the basics: confirm the current address, batch timings and fee directly with the academy, because directory listings in this city are often stale.

Quick Comparison: Dance Academies in Chandigarh

Detailed Reviews of Dance Academies in Chandigarh

1. Pracheen Kala Kendra

Pracheen Kala Kendra is the city's classical institution rather than a commercial studio. Its own website states it was established in 1956 by Guru M. L. Koser and Dr Shobha Koser, and that it works as an affiliating and examining body for Indian classical music, dance and fine arts, training students under the guru-shishya tradition.

For a learner who wants graded certification in a classical form, this is the clearest route in Chandigarh: its examination page lists Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Manipuri, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Tagore Dance, examined through a set ladder of certificates and diplomas. The Kendra also runs Monthly Baithaks, its long-running series of cultural programmes.

  • Based in Sector 35-B, Chandigarh (directory listings).
  • Founded in 1956, per the Kendra's own website; registered in 1957 under the Societies Act.
  • Dance subjects examined: Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Manipuri, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Tagore Dance.
  • Course ladder: Prarambhik, then Bhushan, Visharad, Bhaskar and Churamani.
  • The Kendra describes a network of 3,800+ affiliated centres on its homepage.
  • Its 300th Monthly Baithak was held in October 2024, per its own history page.

2. Dance World

Dance World was a large Sector 17 academy: its own listing description calls it Chandigarh's first and largest dance training institute, founded in April 2006, and The Indian Express has reported its training in Salsa, Hip-Hop, Bhangra, Rumba, Samba and Tango, naming Rajiv Garg as its director.

One caution matters here. The academy's Google listing is currently marked “Permanently Closed”, so treat this entry as a record of a well-known academy rather than a confirmed running one, and check its official channel before planning a visit.

  • Listed in Sector 17, near Neelam Theatre (directory listings; the exact SCO number conflicts between sources).
  • Founding in April 2006 is the academy's own listing claim, not independently confirmed.
  • Styles reported by The Indian Express: Salsa, Hip-Hop, Bhangra, Rumba, Samba and Tango.
  • Director named by The Indian Express: Rajiv Garg.
  • Current Google listing status: permanently closed.

3. Rock ’N’ Roll Dance Institute

Rock N Roll, in Sector 35-D, combines dance classes with fitness, modelling and acting under one roof. Its own website lists Zumba, yoga and pilates alongside dance, and claims it is the only studio in Chandigarh running Salsa, Bachata and Kizomba classes on weekdays, which is the academy's own claim.

Its own channels describe classes for beginners, kids, adults and couples, and name Ajay Bali as its Zumba instructor (ZIN); a kids' modelling video on its channel names him as founder. No founding year could be verified from the academy itself, so none is stated here.

  • Address from its own channels: SCO 288, First Floor, Sector 35-D.
  • Dance styles on its own channels include Salsa, Bachata, Kizomba, Bollywood and dedicated kids' classes.
  • Fitness on its own website: Zumba, yoga and pilates, including ladies' dance-fitness sessions.
  • Also offers modelling and acting classes, per its own website.

4. Jaskshan’s Dance Dacha

Dance Dacha is built around its founder. The academy's own description names Jasmeet K. Shan, a State Gold Champion of the Latin American Dance Sport Championship with a postgraduate degree in communication studies, as the founder, and says the studio teaches folk, classical and casual dance forms under one roof, with training in choreography and improvisation.

Its programme range is unusually wide: its own description lists programmes for beginners through advanced levels, plus special programmes for housewives, senior citizens and special-needs children, and licensed Zumba Fitness sessions. Listings place the studio in Sector 9-C.

  • Founder: Jasmeet K. Shan, per the academy's own description.
  • Listed address: SCO 143-144, First Floor, Madhya Marg, Sector 9-C (listings).
  • Forms named in its own description: folk, classical and casual dancing.
  • Licensed Zumba Fitness sessions, per its own description.
  • Programmes for housewives, senior citizens and special-needs children, per its own description.

5. Chandigarh Dance Academy

Chandigarh Dance Academy's own website keeps things simple: it offers dance classes and event choreography, and lists its styles as classical, folk, Bollywood, western, hip hop, salsa, contemporary, ballet and more. The same homepage says admissions are open to male and female learners of any age group.

Directory listings place its batches at the Stepping Stones School Campus in Sector 38-A. Beyond the academy's own one-page site and those listings, public information is thin, and no founding year or named head could be verified from the academy itself.

  • Styles on the academy's own website: classical, folk, Bollywood, western, hip hop, salsa, contemporary and ballet.
  • Event choreography is offered, per its own website.
  • Open to any age group, per its own website.
  • Location at Stepping Stones School Campus, Sector 38-A, is directory-sourced.

6. The ShowStoppers Dance Academy

Directory listings place The ShowStoppers Dance Academy in Sector 37-D, near Stepping Stones School, teaching Locking-Popping, Hip-Hop, Bollywood, Bhangra and Salsa, with wedding choreography listed on WeddingWire. The name is linked to the Chandigarh Showstoppers dance group, whose founder members Abhinav Abrol and Tapvir Virk reached the quarter-finals of India's Got Talent and were Boogie Woogie runners-up in 2008, according to The Indian Express.

Treat its current status carefully: the academy's Facebook place listing is marked “Permanently Closed” even though directories still carry it as active, so confirm directly before relying on it.

  • Listed address: SCO 42, Sector 37-D, near Stepping Stones School (directories).
  • Styles per directories: Locking-Popping, Hip-Hop, Bollywood, Bhangra, Salsa and freestyle forms.
  • Wedding choreography for couples and wedding functions is listed on WeddingWire.
  • The linked Showstoppers group's television record is reported by The Indian Express; the academy's own founding year is not verified.
  • Current operating status is uncertain: its Facebook place listing says permanently closed.

7. Freedom2Dance Studio

Freedom2Dance is Chandigarh's Latin-leaning studio. Directory listings describe LA Style Salsa, Sensual Bachata, Kizomba and Latin ballroom technique, alongside contemporary and Bollywood fitness, with an emphasis on couple partnering. Reviews reproduced by directories name Vipul Sharma as the studio's director and choreographer, and its official presence is a Facebook page rather than a website.

Listings say it teaches kids, teens and adults from beginner to advanced level, in group and private settings, with sessions that blend dance and aerobic exercise. Its Sector 32-D listing is shown as active.

  • Address: SCO 291, Top Floor, Sector 32-D (directories and its Facebook place listing).
  • Signature styles per directories: Salsa, Bachata, Kizomba and Latin ballroom; also contemporary and Bollywood fitness.
  • Teaches kids, teens and adults, beginner to advanced (directory listings).
  • Vipul Sharma is named as director and choreographer in directory-reproduced reviews.
  • A directory dates the studio to 2016; this could not be confirmed on an official site.

8. The Dance Mafia

The Dance Mafia describes itself, in its own video descriptions, as a dance and fitness studio working across Mohali and Chandigarh. Chandigarh listings place it in Sector 44-C, with two further branches in Mohali. Secondary sources say it was launched by Ripanpreet Sidhu, a Boogie Woogie finalist, and its own channel credits wedding choreography to Sidhu and co-choreographer Deep Birla.

Its own listing text covers a long style list, from Western, Jazz and Hip-Hop to Bhangra, Bollywood, Belly Dance, Salsa and B-Boying, and the studio promotes wedding choreography, fitness classes and choreography for school and college annual shows. Directory listings conflict on its founding year, so none is stated.

  • Chandigarh listing: SCO 86, Sector 44-C (Justdial); branches also listed in Mohali Phase 7 and Phase 5.
  • Founder: Ripanpreet Sidhu, a Boogie Woogie finalist, per secondary sources and WeddingWire.
  • Styles in its own listing text: Western, Jazz, Hip-Hop, Bhangra, Locking-Popping, Bollywood, Belly Dance, Salsa, Cha-Cha-Cha, B-Boying and aerobics.
  • Fitness classes include Zumba and aerobics, per secondary listings.
  • Wedding choreography and school/college annual-show choreography, per its own channel.
  • An UrbanPro profile line claims teaching ages 3 to 70 (directory-sourced).

9. The Danza Land

Current listings place The Danza Land in Sector 34-A; older guides list it in Sector 16-D, which points to a relocation rather than two branches. Directory profiles name its instructor as Addy, a choreographer described as trained across many dance forms, and say classes cater to all age groups from beginner to advanced.

Its style list in directory guides is broad, covering hip-hop, jazz, salsa, contemporary, urban bhangra and Bollywood among others, and the studio is described as specialising in contemporary dance. Two directories date it to 2018, but no official website could be found to confirm that year.

  • Current listed address: SCO 80, First Floor, Sector 34-A; older guides list Sector 16-D.
  • Instructor named in directory profiles: Addy.
  • Classes for all ages, beginner to advanced (directory listings).
  • Styles per directory guides: hip-hop, tricking, locking, jazz, jazz-funk, salsa, contemporary, dancehall, urban bhangra, Bollywood and party dance.
  • Founding year 2018 rests on directory sources only.

10. PDA Pals Dancing Arena

Pals Dancing Arena has the fullest public record of any academy on this list, through its own website. It states the studio was founded by Himanshu Pal, who left a career in law for dance, and that it has been running for over five years. Its batches include kids' classes for ages 4 to 12, built on rhythm, coordination and confidence.

Its own site lists hip-hop in its full street vocabulary of breaking, popping, locking and freestyle, plus an intermediate-to-advanced choreography batch, funk jazz and contemporary. It also runs Zumba and yoga, a ladies' batch, workshops by visiting national choreographers, studio hire, and choreography for weddings, anniversaries and religious events.

  • Address: SCO 2415-2416, First Floor, Sector 22-C (directories, matching its social listing).
  • Founder: Himanshu Pal, per the academy's own website.
  • Kids' batches for ages 4 to 12, per its own website.
  • Styles on its own website: hip-hop, contemporary and funk jazz, plus choreography batches.
  • Fitness on its own website: Zumba and yoga; a dedicated ladies' batch.
  • Wedding, anniversary and religious-event choreography, per its own website.
  • The studio is also offered for external workshop bookings, with a sprung floor and full-wall mirrors.

11. DanceworkZ Studio

DanceworkZ presents itself mainly as a wedding choreography studio. Its WeddingWire listing describes it as a Chandigarh wedding choreography provider for pre-wedding, wedding and post-wedding functions, covering choreography for the couple and for friends and family, song selection and track mixing, with training sessions at the studio, at the client's venue or online.

The genres it lists for wedding work are Bollywood, Punjabi, old Hindi songs, contemporary and hip-hop, and its own Facebook-linked place listing also mentions Zumba fitness classes and dance home tuition. Public information about its regular class batches is limited, and claims about its founders that circulate on blog lists could not be corroborated, so they are not repeated here.

  • Listed address: SCO 37, Top Floor, Sector 18-D (its Facebook place listing and WeddingWire).
  • Main service per WeddingWire: wedding and sangeet choreography, including song selection and track mixing.
  • Training at the studio, at the client site, or online (WeddingWire).
  • Wedding genres listed: Bollywood, Punjabi, old Hindi songs, contemporary and hip-hop.
  • Zumba classes and dance home tuition are mentioned in its own place listing.
  • Note: another studio in this guide, Uma Dance Studio, lists the same SCO 37, Sector 18-D address.

12. The Dance Unity

The Dance Unity is a dance and fitness studio in Sector 21-C. Its own Instagram bio names Aryan Suryavanshi as director and choreographer, an UrbanPro listing states he founded the studio, and its own videos credit its choreography to him. A local guide notes it began under the name Beat Breakers and provides classes for novices.

Wedding work is a clear part of its offer: its WeddingWire listing covers choreography for couples and for friends and family, song selection and track mixing, across Bollywood, Punjabi, old Hindi songs, contemporary and hip-hop, with training at the studio, at the venue or online. The studio describes itself as a Global Achievers Award 2017 winner in its own listing text.

  • Address: SCO 31, Top Floor, Sector 21-C, from its own Instagram bio and WeddingWire.
  • Director and choreographer: Aryan Suryavanshi, per its own Instagram bio.
  • Classes for novices and beginners, per a local guide; reviewers describe batches for all ages.
  • Wedding choreography services per WeddingWire, including travel outside the city.
  • “Global Achievers Award 2017” is the studio's own self-description in its listing.

13. Urban School of Dance

Urban School of Dance appears in older Chandigarh academy lists with a wide style range: Bhangra, Bollywood, Jazz, Salsa, Contemporary, Kizomba, Bachata and Ballroom, taught, according to one list, by international trainers. That is where the reliable record ends.

Its addresses conflict between listings, Sector 20-C in some and Sector 8-C in another, and both place listings found in this research mark it “Permanently Closed”. It is kept in this guide for completeness, but on current public evidence it should not be treated as a running academy without a fresh check.

  • Styles in older lists: Bhangra, Bollywood, Jazz, Salsa, Contemporary, Kizomba, Bachata and Ballroom (blog-sourced).
  • No official website or official social page could be found.
  • Addresses in listings conflict: Sector 20-C and Sector 8-C.
  • Current status: place listings mark it permanently closed; limited public information.

14. The Dance Studio

The Dance Studio is the hardest entry in this guide to document. The only source found that names it is a single local blog list, which places it at SCO 41, Sector 8-C and describes classes in contemporary, ballet and hip-hop for beginners and advanced dancers.

No official website, official social page or directory listing under this name and address could be found to corroborate that entry, and the blog in question reuses contact details across its listings. This profile is therefore marked as limited public information: confirm the studio directly before relying on it.

  • Single-source listing: SCO 41, Sector 8-C (one local blog list, uncorroborated).
  • Styles in that listing: contemporary, ballet and hip-hop.
  • Levels in that listing: beginners and advanced dancers.
  • No official page or directory listing could be verified; limited public information.

15. Uma Dance Studio

Uma Dance Studio's public footprint is its Instagram presence. In the self-description carried on its listing, the studio gives its own address as SCO-37, First Floor, Sector 18-D, and describes itself with the words dancer, choreographer, artist and director, without naming a person.

Posts summarised in its listing refer to workshops and to Bollywood-style practice sessions, but no formal list of styles, class batches or services is published anywhere that could be found. One practical note: DanceworkZ Studio, earlier in this guide, lists the same SCO 37, Sector 18-D address, so check which studio is currently at the premises before visiting. Beyond this, public information is limited.

  • Address from its own self-description: SCO-37, First Floor, Sector 18-D.
  • Official presence found: an Instagram account, @uma_dance_studio.
  • Workshop posts and Bollywood-style practice posts appear in its listing summaries.
  • No founder name, style syllabus or service list is published in the sources found; limited public information.

16. The Karma Dance Studio

The Karma Dance Studio is listed at Kundan International School in Sector 46-B. Its directory description says it offers classes from ballet and jazz to hip-hop and contemporary, for dancers of all ages and skill levels, from first-time beginners to advanced dancers.

It also appears in WedMeGood's Chandigarh sangeet-choreographer listings. No official website or official social page for the studio could be found, and the style list above comes from a directory description whose wording is reused across other studios' listings, so treat it as directory-stated rather than academy-confirmed and check the current schedule with the school or studio directly.

  • Listed address: Kundan International School, Sector-46B, Chandi Path (Google and directory listings).
  • Styles in its directory description: ballet, jazz, hip-hop and contemporary.
  • All ages and skill levels, per the same directory description.
  • Listed among Chandigarh sangeet choreographers on WedMeGood.
  • No official site or social page could be verified.

17. Rockstar Academy

Rockstar Academy operates from the AKSIPS campus in Sector 45-A, with a head office also listed in Mohali. Directory listings give it a wide style list, including hip-hop, locking and popping, Kathak, salsa, Bollywood and bhangra, and say it offers professional choreography for corporate events, weddings, school functions and college festivals, alongside acting, aerobics and yoga under its full academy name.

Local press coverage of its students names Sameer Mahajan as founder-owner and dance director, and Sakshi Rauthan as managing director and choreographer. The same reporting describes twin students who have trained at the academy since the age of four winning first position at the Dance World Cup in Bengaluru in 2023 and further titles in Europe in 2024. No founding year could be verified.

  • Chandigarh base: AKSIPS, Sector 45-A (directory listings); a head office is also listed in Mohali.
  • Styles per directories: hip-hop, locking and popping, Kathak, salsa, Bollywood, bhangra, break dance, jazz, jive and freestyle forms.
  • Event choreography for corporate events, weddings, school functions and college festivals (directory listings).
  • Founder-owner and dance director Sameer Mahajan, and MD and choreographer Sakshi Rauthan, are named in local press.
  • Its students' Dance World Cup Bengaluru 2023 win and 2024 European titles are reported by local press.
  • Do not confuse it with Rock 'N' Roll Dance Institute in Sector 35-D, a different academy.

18. Oorja Danceworks

Oorja Danceworks was founded in Chandigarh in 2016 by Devanshi Mishra, a Kathak-trained dancer who holds a National Scholarship for Dance from the Government of India; both the founding year and the founder are stated by Toronto Dance Theatre and Dance Umbrella of Ontario. Its Chandigarh base was in Sector 40-B, and Chandigarh-era listings describe accredited classes in Bollywood, Indian contemporary, hip-hop, freestyle, Masala Bhangra and Zumba for all age groups, plus Kathak in the Jaipur Gharana tradition and wedding choreography listings.

The honest caveat is that Oorja has moved. Its own website now presents it as a Toronto studio, and its Chandigarh Google listing is marked permanently closed, so do not assume Sector 40 classes are still running; contact the studio to ask about any current Chandigarh teaching or online options.

  • Founded in Chandigarh in 2016 by Devanshi Mishra (Toronto Dance Theatre artist biography).
  • Chandigarh base was Quiet Office 7, Sector 40-B (UrbanPro listing).
  • Styles in its own descriptions: Indian contemporary, Bollywood, jazz, belly dance, Kathak, hip-hop, Zumba, folk fitness and Masala Bhangra.
  • Wedding and sangeet choreography was listed on WedMeGood for Chandigarh.
  • Current status: its own website is Toronto-based and the Chandigarh listing is marked permanently closed.

19. Steps Growing Academy

Steps Growing Academy is a multi-skill academy in Sector 30-A covering acting, modelling and dance. Its UrbanPro listing text describes it as a Chandigarh academy for acting, modelling and dance since 2014, offering basic to advanced courses for kids to adults.

Its Justdial service menu lists beginner, advanced and individual dance classes, and wedding choreography classes. That is the extent of its public record: no official website, official social page or named founder could be found, so this profile rests on directory sources only and its details should be confirmed with the academy directly.

  • Sector 30-A, Chandigarh (Justdial and UrbanPro listings).
  • Acting, modelling and dance under one academy, per its UrbanPro listing text.
  • “Since 2014” and basic-to-advanced courses for kids to adults are from its own UrbanPro listing text.
  • Beginner, advanced and individual dance classes, plus wedding choreography classes, appear on its Justdial service menu.
  • No founder or official page could be verified; limited public information.

20. Gurdeep Singh Academy

Gurdeep Singh Academy, which trades as GSA, teaches Salsa, Bachata, Bhangra and Bollywood, and its listing name adds dance fitness to that list. Its detailed Justdial listing places the academy in Lohgarh, Zirakpur, which makes it a Tricity academy rather than a Chandigarh-sector studio; a Google listing with the same phone number and Instagram handle also places it at Rainbow International School in Chandigarh, and a second listing gives an address in Singhpura, Zirakpur.

Justdial describes its classes as open to individuals of all ages and levels, and states a year of establishment of 2020, which rests on that directory alone. Reviews on the listing name the teacher as Gurdeep Singh; no source explicitly gives him a founder title.

  • Main detailed listing: Lohgarh, Zirakpur, near Sigma City Chowk (Justdial); a Chandigarh listing at Rainbow International School shares its phone and Instagram.
  • Styles: Salsa, Bachata, Bhangra and Bollywood (Justdial name and reviews).
  • Dance fitness is part of its own listing name.
  • Classes for all ages and levels, per Justdial.
  • Year of establishment 2020 is stated by Justdial only.
  • Official presence: Instagram, @gurdeepsinghacademy; no standalone website found.

Also Worth Knowing About Dance Classes in Chandigarh

Two patterns run through this guide and are worth knowing before you choose. First, several well-known names are in transition: Dance World and Urban School of Dance are marked permanently closed in their place listings, The ShowStoppers Academy's status conflicts between sources, and Oorja Danceworks now operates from Toronto. None of that erases their record, but it does mean a phone call beats an unannounced visit.

Second, Chandigarh's dance scene is increasingly specialist. Wedding choreography is now a service in its own right, with studios such as DanceworkZ and The Dance Unity offering song selection and track mixing alongside teaching, while fitness-led formats such as Zumba sit inside most larger studios' timetables. Choosing by specialism, rather than by the biggest name, usually gives the better fit.

FAQs About Dance Academies in Chandigarh

Which is the best dance academy in Chandigarh for classical dance?

Pracheen Kala Kendra in Sector 35-B is the specialist choice: it is an examining body in its own right, teaching Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Manipuri, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Tagore Dance through a graded ladder from Prarambhik to Churamani. Rockstar Academy and Oorja Danceworks have also listed Kathak, but neither offers the Kendra's examination structure.

What dance styles can I learn in Chandigarh?

Between the academies in this guide, the city covers Indian classical forms, Bollywood, hip-hop and street styles, bhangra and folk, contemporary and jazz, ballet, and Latin forms including Salsa, Bachata and Kizomba. Rock N Roll in Sector 35-D and Freedom2Dance in Sector 32-D are the most Latin-focused listings.

Are there dance classes for kids in Chandigarh?

Yes. Pals Dancing Arena runs dedicated kids' batches for ages 4 to 12, Rock N Roll describes kids' classes on its own channels, and The Danza Land, The Dance Mafia and Steps Growing Academy all describe classes spanning children to adults in their listings. Age bands vary, so confirm the exact batch for your child's age with the academy.

Do Chandigarh dance academies offer wedding choreography?

Several specialise in it. DanceworkZ and The Dance Unity build their listings around wedding and sangeet choreography, including song selection and track mixing, and Pals Dancing Arena, The Dance Mafia, The ShowStoppers and Steps Growing Academy all list wedding work as well. Sessions are commonly offered at the studio, at your venue or online, per the listings.

How much do dance classes in Chandigarh cost?

There is no reliable single answer, and this guide does not print fee figures: the academies' own pages do not publish consistent fee tables, and the figures in directory round-ups could not be verified against the academies themselves. Ask the academy directly about its monthly fee, joining fee and trial-class policy before you commit; most run trial or demo sessions that make the comparison easier.

How do I check an academy is still running before I visit?

Check its official social page for recent posts, then call or message before travelling. This matters in Chandigarh because several listings in this guide, including Dance World, Urban School of Dance and Oorja Danceworks' Chandigarh listing, are marked permanently closed in place listings even where older articles still recommend them, and two studios list the same Sector 18-D address.

Conclusion

For certified classical training, Pracheen Kala Kendra stands apart; for children, weddings, Latin styles and fitness-led classes, the profiles above name the academies whose own pages and listings support the claim. Whichever you choose, verify the current address, batch and fee with the academy itself, because in this city the listings age faster than the dancing does.

India's chocolate shelf has never been wider. A single supermarket aisle now holds the milk-chocolate bars most of us grew up with, Swiss and Belgian imports, American peanut and caramel bars, and a new wave of Indian craft chocolate made from cacao grown in Andhra Pradesh. This guide profiles fifteen chocolate brands sold in India — who owns them, where they come from, what each one is known for, and who it suits best.

This is an editorial selection, not an official ranking. The order below is not a league table, and we have not used sales figures or market shares to arrange it. Availability varies by city: some brands are in every kirana store in the country, while others are found mainly in metro supermarkets, premium stores and online. Use the profiles to match a brand to your taste — milk chocolate, dark and single-origin bars, gifting boxes or wafer and biscuit bars — and then check what your local stores stock.

Milk, Dark or White: What the Names Mean

The words on the wrapper describe the recipe. Milk chocolate contains milk solids as well as cocoa, which is why it tastes creamy and sweet. Dark chocolate carries a higher share of cocoa and little or no milk, so it tastes more intense and less sweet. White chocolate is made with cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, which is why it is pale and tastes of milk and vanilla rather than of cocoa.

None of the three is automatically better than the others — it is a question of taste and occasion. A milk-chocolate bar is the everyday default for most Indian shoppers; dark chocolate suits those who like a stronger cocoa flavour; and white chocolate works best in bars and fillings where its creamy sweetness is the point. The habit worth building is simple: read the wrapper for the cocoa content and the ingredients before you buy, especially if you are buying for children or for someone who avoids milk.

Quick Answer: The 15 Brands at a Glance

  • Cadbury Dairy Milk — India's default milk chocolate; the 1905 classic from Cadbury, now part of Mondelez.
  • Amul — the Gujarat cooperative's chocolate range; dark, milk and fruit-and-nut bars at everyday prices.
  • Cadbury 5 Star — caramel and nougat in a chocolate coat; an India favourite since 1969.
  • Toblerone — the Swiss triangular bar of honey and almond nougat, made since 1908.
  • Ferrero Rocher — the golden hazelnut praline; the go-to gifting chocolate since 1982.
  • Snickers — peanuts, nougat and caramel from Mars; in India since 2008.
  • Galaxy — Mars's smooth milk chocolate, made in Britain since 1960 and sold in India.
  • Twix — caramel and biscuit in chocolate; a Mars bar on sale in Britain since 1967.
  • Maltesers — malted-milk centres in milk chocolate; a Mars classic first sold in 1937.
  • Orion Choco Pie — the Korean marshmallow cake coated in chocolate, created in 1974.
  • Loacker — Italian wafers from South Tyrol; the Napolitaner hazelnut wafer is the signature.
  • Fabelle — ITC's luxury chocolate, launched in 2016 and sold through its hotel boutiques.
  • Godiva — the Belgian chocolatier founded in Brussels in 1926; truffles and pralines.
  • Manam Chocolate — Hyderabad craft chocolate, bean-to-bar with Indian cacao.
  • Smoor — Bengaluru's couverture chocolate brand, founded in 2015, with lounges across India.

The Brands in Detail

1. Cadbury Dairy Milk

Cadbury Dairy Milk is the bar most of India means when it says "chocolate". Cadbury itself was founded in Birmingham in 1824 by John Cadbury, and Dairy Milk was launched in 1905 at Bournville, made with a higher proportion of milk than earlier chocolate bars. Cadbury began operating in India in 1948, and the brand is now part of Mondelez International, with its India business headquartered in Mumbai.

The range is the widest in this guide: the classic Dairy Milk bar, Fruit & Nut, Roast Almond, Crackle, Silk and its many gift packs, plus the brand's long-running "Kuch Meetha Ho Jaaye" line. If you want one chocolate that is easy to find almost anywhere in India — from a metro supermarket to a small-town kirana — Dairy Milk is the practical first choice.

  • Brand owner: Mondelez International (Cadbury)
  • Since: Dairy Milk launched 1905; Cadbury founded 1824
  • Known for: classic milk chocolate, Silk, Fruit & Nut, Roast Almond, gift packs
  • Best for: everyday eating, sharing and gifting

Check Cadbury Dairy Milk on Amazon

2. Amul

Amul is the brand of the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), the Anand-based federation of dairy cooperatives whose roots go back to 1946. The same cooperative structure behind India's best-known milk and butter also makes its chocolate, and that is why Amul chocolate is stocked almost everywhere dairy is sold.

The chocolate range covers the everyday ground well: milk chocolate, dark chocolate, fruit and nut, and the small Chocominis, all under the "The Taste of India" banner the brand has carried for decades. Choose Amul when you want a dependable, widely available Indian chocolate at an everyday price — and a dark chocolate that is easy to find in any Indian town.

  • Brand owner: GCMMF (dairy cooperative federation)
  • Base: Anand, Gujarat
  • Known for: milk, dark and fruit-and-nut chocolate bars, Chocominis
  • Best for: everyday Indian chocolate at honest prices

3. Cadbury 5 Star

5 Star is Cadbury's caramel-and-nougat bar, and it is one of the most Indian of all the brands in this guide: it was launched in India in 1969 as a bar that was hard outside with soft caramel nougat inside, and it has stayed a fixture of Indian pockets and lunchboxes ever since. It is owned by Mondelez International, like Dairy Milk.

The original bar is still the core of the range, joined over the years by variants such as 5 Star Crunchy, 5 Star Oreo and 5 Star 3D, and by the brand's cheerful "Eat 5 Star, Do Nothing" advertising. Pick 5 Star when you want a chewy, filling bar rather than a plain slab of chocolate — it is the countline for a hungry moment, not a tasting exercise.

  • Brand owner: Mondelez International (Cadbury)
  • Launched in India: 1969
  • Known for: caramel and nougat bar; Crunchy, Oreo and 3D variants
  • Best for: a filling, chewy snack bar

4. Toblerone

Toblerone is the most recognisable shape in chocolate: the triangular prism created in Bern, Switzerland, in 1908 by Theodor Tobler. The bar is milk chocolate with honey and almond nougat, and its name blends Tobler with "torrone", the Italian word for nougat. It is now owned by Mondelez International.

In India, Toblerone is the classic travel and gifting bar — the one bought at airports and duty-free shops and carried home in the distinctive yellow pack. The range also includes dark, white and fruit-and-nut versions, and the small "Tiny" pieces that suit sharing. Choose it when the bar itself is part of the gift.

  • Brand owner: Mondelez International
  • Created: 1908, Bern, Switzerland
  • Known for: triangular milk chocolate with honey and almond nougat
  • Best for: gifting and travel purchases

Check Toblerone on Amazon

5. Ferrero Rocher

Ferrero Rocher is the golden ball that has become shorthand for a premium gift in India. It was launched in 1982 by the Ferrero Group, the Italian confectioner founded in 1946 in Alba, Italy, by Pietro Ferrero. Each piece is a whole hazelnut in a hazelnut praline filling, wrapped in a crisp wafer shell, coated in milk chocolate and chopped hazelnuts.

The brand is built for occasions: the gold-wrapped pieces come in boxes of 3, 16 and 24 that are made to be handed over at Diwali, weddings and festivals. Ferrero Rocher also sells bars and the smaller Moments range for everyday eating. If the chocolate is a gift first and a snack second, this is the safest premium choice in India.

  • Brand owner: Ferrero Group
  • Launched: 1982; Ferrero founded 1946, Alba, Italy
  • Known for: golden hazelnut pralines in gift boxes; Moments range
  • Best for: festive and formal gifting

Check Ferrero Rocher on Amazon

6. Snickers

Snickers is Mars's answer to hunger: peanuts, nougat and caramel under milk chocolate, introduced in the United States in 1930 and launched in India in 2008. Mars itself was founded in 1911, and Snickers is one of its biggest global brands — the bar that turned a chocolate into a snack.

In India the classic bar is joined by variants such as Butterscotch and Almond, and by Miniatures pouches for sharing. Snickers suits the shopper who wants a bar that actually fills a gap between meals, and it is the natural rival to 5 Star in the countline aisle. Look for the brown pack with the blue-and-red wordmark.

  • Brand owner: Mars, Incorporated
  • Introduced: 1930 (USA); in India since 2008
  • Known for: peanut, nougat and caramel bar; Butterscotch and Almond variants
  • Best for: a filling snack bar

Check Snickers on Amazon

7. Galaxy

Galaxy is Mars's smooth milk chocolate, first manufactured in Britain in 1960. It is sold as Galaxy in India, Britain and much of the world, and under the name Dove in the United States. The brand's whole pitch is smoothness: a softer, creamier milk chocolate than the average bar.

The Indian range centres on the Smooth Milk bar, with Caramel, Cookie Crumble and Fruit & Nut alongside, plus Minstrels and Ripple in the wider family. Galaxy suits shoppers who find ordinary milk chocolate a little harsh and want something gentler — a quiet, creamy bar rather than a loud one.

  • Brand owner: Mars, Incorporated
  • Introduced: 1960, United Kingdom
  • Known for: smooth milk chocolate; Caramel, Cookie Crumble, Fruit & Nut
  • Best for: lovers of soft, creamy milk chocolate

8. Twix

Twix is the biscuit bar of the Mars family: a crunchy biscuit finger topped with caramel and coated in milk chocolate, sold as two fingers in a pack. It went on sale in Britain in 1967, and was sold as Raider in some European markets until the name was unified as Twix in 1991.

Twix is at its best as a tea-time bar — the biscuit gives it a crunch that pure chocolate bars do not have, and the two-finger pack is made for sharing (or not). The range includes the larger Xtra bar for a bigger appetite. Choose Twix when you want chocolate with a biscuit in it, rather than chocolate alone.

  • Brand owner: Mars, Incorporated
  • Introduced: 1967, United Kingdom
  • Known for: caramel and biscuit fingers; Twix Xtra
  • Best for: tea-time snacking and sharing

9. Maltesers

Maltesers are milk-chocolate balls with a light, crunchy malted-milk centre — a combination Mars has sold since the bar was created by Forrest Mars Sr. at the company's Slough factory in 1936 and first sold in 1937. They were originally marketed as a lighter chocolate, and the airy centre still makes them feel less heavy than a solid chocolate ball.

In India, Maltesers come in shareable pouches and boxes, and the brand has also spun off the Teasers chocolate bar, which folds the malt balls into a bar. They suit film nights and sharing bowls, where a handful at a time is the whole point.

  • Brand owner: Mars, Incorporated
  • First sold: 1937, United Kingdom
  • Known for: malted-milk centres in milk chocolate; Teasers bar
  • Best for: sharing pouches and film nights

10. Orion Choco Pie

Choco Pie is the odd one out in this guide, and that is its charm: it is not a bar at all, but a soft marshmallow filling sandwiched between two small cakes and coated in chocolate. It was created in 1974 in South Korea by Orion, then known as Tongyang Confectionery, and the company behind it was founded in 1956.

In India, Choco Pie is sold as an individually wrapped snack cake — a lunchbox and tea-time favourite that children and adults both reach for. It is the gentlest chocolate in this list, and the best choice when you want something soft and cakey rather than a hard bar.

  • Brand owner: Orion Corporation, South Korea
  • Created: 1974
  • Known for: marshmallow sandwich cake coated in chocolate
  • Best for: lunchboxes, tea-time snacks and soft textures

11. Loacker

Loacker is the Italian wafer specialist of this guide. The family business was founded in 1925 in Bolzano, in South Tyrol in the Italian Alps, and it still makes its wafers there, in the shadow of the mountains pictured on its red shield logo. The signature product is the Napolitaner wafer — crisp wafers layered with hazelnut cream.

The range sold in India includes the Classic wafer fingers, the bite-size Quadratini cubes and chocolate-coated wafers. Loacker suits shoppers who like their chocolate light and crisp rather than dense, and it is the best wafer in this guide by a distance.

  • Brand owner: Loacker (family-owned)
  • Founded: 1925, Bolzano, Italy
  • Known for: Napolitaner hazelnut wafers, Classic wafers, Quadratini
  • Best for: light, crisp wafer chocolate

12. Fabelle

Fabelle is ITC's luxury chocolate brand, and the most Indian premium name in this guide. It was launched in 2016, with its first chocolate boutique opening at ITC Gardenia in Bengaluru in April that year, and it is sold through boutiques in ITC's luxury hotels as well as in premium retail. The brand's master chocolatiers work with single-origin cacaos from regions such as Ghana, Madagascar, Colombia and Venezuela.

The luxury range covers handcrafted pralines, ganache and truffles, while the mass-premium range launched in 2018 offers centre-filled bars and the multi-layered Choco Deck bars in supermarkets. Fabelle is the pick for a genuinely Indian luxury gift — and for anyone who wants to taste single-origin chocolate without importing it.

  • Brand owner: ITC Limited
  • Launched: 2016, Bengaluru
  • Known for: handcrafted pralines and ganache; single-origin cacaos; Choco Deck bars
  • Best for: luxury gifting and single-origin tasting

"Craft the finest luxury chocolates in India that rival the best in the world."

— ITC, on the launch of Fabelle, May 2016

13. Godiva

Godiva is the Belgian chocolatier of this guide, founded in Brussels in 1926 by Pierre Draps and named after Lady Godiva. The company is now headquartered in New York and owned by Yildiz Holding, but its identity is still Belgian: pralines, truffles and the gold Ballotin gift box.

In India, Godiva sells through boutiques in the big metros and through premium online stores, which makes it a special-occasion purchase rather than an everyday one. Its truffles and assorted praline boxes are the classic choice for a formal gift — the box that says the giver thought about it.

  • Brand owner: Godiva Chocolatier (Yildiz Holding)
  • Founded: 1926, Brussels, Belgium
  • Known for: truffles, pralines and the gold Ballotin gift box
  • Best for: formal and premium gifting

14. Manam Chocolate

Manam is the new face of Indian chocolate. Founded in Hyderabad in 2021 by entrepreneur Chaitanya Muppala, the brand launched publicly in August 2023 and works bean-to-bar: its parent company, Distinct Origins, works with more than 250 farmers growing fine-flavour cacao in Andhra Pradesh's West Godavari district, and ferments and makes the chocolate in India.

Its Hyderabad "Karkhana" was named one of TIME magazine's World's Greatest Places in 2024, and the range runs from single-origin tablets and bonbons to truffles, spreads and drinking chocolate. Manam is the pick for readers who want to taste what Indian cacao can do — and to support the craft chocolate movement at its source.

  • Brand owner: Manam Chocolate (Distinct Origins Pvt. Ltd.)
  • Founded: 2021, Hyderabad; brand launched August 2023
  • Known for: bean-to-bar tablets, bonbons and truffles from Indian cacao
  • Best for: craft chocolate lovers and single-origin tasting

15. Smoor

Smoor is Bengaluru's couverture chocolate brand, founded in 2015 by Vimal Sharma. It began as a small operation making couverture chocolate — the higher-cocoa-butter chocolate professionals use — more accessible in India, and has grown into a chain of chocolate lounges and stores across Indian cities, with its own retail and online sales.

The range covers handcrafted truffles, chocolate bars, cakes and desserts, and the brand has recently added an Indian-origin cacao range made bean-to-bar from cacao grown in Andhra Pradesh. Smoor suits shoppers who want a cafe-and-store experience with their chocolate, and a reliable source of truffles and celebration cakes.

  • Brand owner: Smoor Chocolates
  • Founded: 2015, Bengaluru
  • Known for: couverture chocolate, truffles, bars and chocolate lounges
  • Best for: truffles, desserts and the lounge experience

Brand Comparison Table

BrandOwnerSinceKnown forBest for
Cadbury Dairy MilkMondelez1905Classic milk chocolate, SilkEveryday eating and gifting

Cadbury 5 StarMondelez1969Caramel and nougat barFilling snack bar

How to Choose a Chocolate Brand

Start with the occasion. Everyday snacking calls for Dairy Milk, Amul, 5 Star or Snickers; gifting calls for Ferrero Rocher, Toblerone, Fabelle or Godiva; and a tasting calls for Manam, Smoor or a dark bar from Amul. Buy the chocolate for the moment, not the other way round.

Match the texture to your taste. If you like smooth and creamy, reach for Galaxy or Dairy Milk Silk. If you want crunch, pick Twix, Loacker or Maltesers. If you want chew, 5 Star and Snickers are the bars for you — and if you want something soft, Choco Pie is the only cakey option in this list.

Check the cocoa content before you pay more. A premium bar should tell you its cocoa percentage on the wrapper; a luxury praline box should name its origin. The craft brands in this guide — Manam, Smoor and Fabelle — all do this, and it is the simplest way to tell a thoughtful chocolate from a merely expensive one.

Buy the right size for the job. Single bars suit personal snacking; pouches and Miniatures suit sharing; and the 16- and 24-piece boxes from Ferrero Rocher and the gift packs from Dairy Milk and Toblerone are made for festivals and family occasions. A big box bought for one person is rarely good value once it has been open a week.

Store it cool and dry. Chocolate keeps best in a cool, dry place away from sunlight — not in a warm kitchen and, in Indian summers, not in a hot car. If a bar turns pale on the surface, it has bloomed: it is still safe to eat, but the texture will have changed, so eat it soon or melt it into a dessert.

FAQs

Which is the best chocolate brand in India?

There is no single answer — it depends on taste and occasion. Cadbury Dairy Milk is the most widely available and the default everyday choice; Amul is the best-value Indian brand; Ferrero Rocher and Fabelle lead on gifting; and Manam and Smoor are the names to know for craft chocolate. This guide is an editorial selection to help you choose, not an official ranking.

Which chocolate is best for gifting?

For festive and family gifting, Ferrero Rocher boxes, Toblerone bars and Cadbury Dairy Milk gift packs are the safe choices. For a premium gift, Fabelle's praline boxes and Godiva's Ballotin are the formal options. For a thoughtful, distinctly Indian gift, a Manam single-origin tablet is hard to beat.

Which brands are best for dark chocolate lovers?

Amul's dark chocolate is the easiest dark bar to find across India. For a deeper tasting, try Manam's single-origin dark tablets, Smoor's dark bars or Fabelle's single-origin range — all three name their cacao origin on the pack, which is what dark chocolate lovers should look for.

Are these chocolates vegetarian?

Most chocolate sold in India is vegetarian and carries the green dot, but recipes vary by product — some pralines and filled chocolates contain egg or gelatine. Check the label of the specific product if this matters to you, and look for the green dot on the pack.

What is the difference between milk, dark and white chocolate?

Milk chocolate contains milk solids as well as cocoa and tastes creamy and sweet. Dark chocolate has a higher share of cocoa and little or no milk, so it tastes more intense. White chocolate is made with cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, so it is pale and tastes of milk and vanilla rather than cocoa.

Why does this guide not list prices?

Chocolate prices vary by city, pack size, retailer and season, and change too often for a guide to stay accurate. We link to Amazon India for the brands sold there so you can see the current price before buying.

Conclusion

India's chocolate shelf rewards both loyalty and curiosity. Keep a dependable everyday brand in the cupboard for daily snacking, back your regional and craft champions when you want something made in India, and leave room for the Swiss, Belgian and Italian classics when the occasion calls for a gift. Whichever brand you choose, read the wrapper, store it cool, and share it while it is at its best.

Research note: Brand backgrounds in this guide were checked against the brands' official websites, company histories and reputable profiles in November 2026. Ranges and flavour names are as the brands themselves describe them; availability varies by city. If you spot an error, please contact VisitBest so we can correct it.

Furnishing a home in India used to mean a trip to the local carpenter and a wait of several weeks. Today the choice runs from century-old Indian manufacturers and global flat-pack giants to online custom-furniture start-ups, furniture rental services and luxury boutiques. This guide profiles fifteen furniture brands sold in India — who owns them, where they come from, what each one is known for, and who it suits best.

This is an editorial selection, not an official ranking. The order below is not a league table, and we have not used sales figures or market shares to arrange it. Availability varies by city: some brands have stores in more than a hundred Indian cities, while others sell mainly online or through a handful of boutiques. Use the profiles to match a brand to your home — a first flat, a family living room, a home office or a luxury interior — and check what your local stores stock.

Solid Wood, Flat-Pack or Plastic: What the Names Mean

The words on the label describe how the furniture is made. Solid-wood furniture is cut from whole timber such as sheesham or teak, which is why it is heavy, durable and expensive to repair. Engineered wood is made from wood fibres or particles pressed into boards, which keeps it lighter and cheaper. Flat-pack furniture arrives in boxes for assembly at home, which is how IKEA keeps its prices low and its stores compact.

Moulded plastic furniture is made by injecting molten plastic into a mould, which is why a Nilkamal or Supreme chair is light, stackable and easy to wash. None of these is automatically better than the others — it is a question of room, budget and use. A solid-wood bed suits a permanent bedroom; a flat-pack wardrobe suits a rented flat; and a plastic chair suits a balcony, a classroom or a canteen. Before you pay, check the material, warranty and assembly terms, especially for large pieces.

Quick Answer: The 15 Brands at a Glance

  • Godrej Interio — India's oldest furniture name; home and office furniture from Godrej & Boyce since 1923, Interio division since 2006.
  • Urban Ladder — Bengaluru online-first retailer founded in 2012, now part of Reliance Retail, with stores and a wide home range.
  • IKEA India — the Swedish flat-pack giant, founded in 1943; first Indian store opened in Hyderabad in 2018.
  • Nilkamal — Mumbai's moulded-furniture maker since 1981; the plastic chair in almost every Indian home and office.
  • Durian — Mumbai plywood and furniture house since 1981; sofas, beds and office furniture from its own factories.
  • WoodenStreet — Jaipur custom-furniture brand launched in 2015; solid-wood pieces made to order, sold online and in stores.
  • Evok — Hindware's home-interiors brand, launched in 2008; furniture, furnishings and modular kitchens under one roof.
  • Stanley — Bengaluru luxury leather furniture, begun in 2007; super-premium sofas and beds, listed in 2024.
  • Featherlite — Bengaluru office-furniture specialist since 1965; chairs and workstations for Indian workplaces.
  • HomeTown — the home-furnishing retail chain launched in 2007; furniture and decor for the whole house.
  • Supreme Furniture — Supreme Industries' furniture arm; moulded plastic chairs and tables since 1990–91.
  • Royaloak — Bengaluru value retailer founded in 2010; international-style furniture in more than 200 stores.
  • Furlenco — Bengaluru furniture rental, founded in 2012; rent a furnished home by the month instead of buying.
  • Bent Chair — Delhi design-led brand started in 2016; bold, quirky furniture and decor made in Ambala.
  • Furniturewalla — Mumbai luxury furniture house founded in 1999; premium furniture, lighting and art.

The Brands in Detail

1. Godrej Interio

Godrej Interio is the oldest furniture name in this guide. Its parent, Godrej & Boyce, was founded in Mumbai in 1897 by Ardeshir Godrej and his brother Pirojsha, and began making furniture in 1923 with the Storewel steel cupboard. Godrej Interio was established as a dedicated furniture division in 2006, and it now covers homes, offices, schools and hospitals.

The range is the widest in this guide: beds, wardrobes, sofas, dining sets and modular kitchens for the home, plus the ergonomic office chairs — Curv, Vurv and Prime — that fill Indian workplaces. If you want one brand that can furnish a whole house and a whole office, with service to match, Godrej Interio is the practical first choice.

  • Brand owner: Godrej & Boyce (Godrej Enterprises Group)
  • Since: furniture since 1923; Interio division established 2006
  • Known for: home and office furniture, ergonomic chairs, sofas, wardrobes
  • Best for: furnishing a whole home or office from one brand

Check Godrej Interio dining chairs on Amazon

Check the Godrej Interio Curv ergonomic chair on Amazon

2. Urban Ladder

Urban Ladder is the online-first furniture retailer that taught a generation of Indians to buy sofas on a screen. It was founded in Bengaluru in July 2012 by Ashish Goel and Rajiv Srivatsa, two friends who had struggled to furnish their own rented flats. In November 2020, Reliance Retail acquired a 96% stake in the company, bringing it inside India's largest retail group.

The range covers the whole home — sofas and recliners, beds and wardrobes, dining sets, study tables, mattresses and decor — sold online and through stores in the big metros. Urban Ladder suits shoppers who want a modern look, clear prices and delivery with installation, without visiting a dozen showrooms.

  • Brand owner: Urban Ladder Home Décor Solutions (Reliance Retail)
  • Founded: July 2012, Bengaluru
  • Known for: sofas, beds, dining sets, study furniture, home decor
  • Best for: modern, ready-to-buy furniture with online ordering

3. IKEA India

IKEA is the world's largest furniture retailer, and the youngest Indian arrival in this guide. It was founded in Sweden in 1943 by the seventeen-year-old Ingvar Kamprad, who began as a mail-order business and opened his first store in Älmhult in 1958. IKEA opened its first Indian store in Hyderabad in August 2018, a 400,000 sq ft store with a 1,000-seater restaurant — then its largest anywhere.

The idea is flat-pack: well-designed furniture that ships in boxes, assembles at home and costs little enough for most people to afford. In India the range centres on the classics — the BILLY bookcase, the MALM bed, the LACK table and the KALLAX shelf — alongside kitchen, wardrobe and children's ranges adapted for Indian homes. IKEA suits shoppers who like clean Scandinavian design, honest prices and a day out in a very large store.

  • Brand owner: IKEA (Inter IKEA Group / Ingka Group)
  • Founded: 1943, Sweden; first India store Hyderabad, August 2018
  • Known for: flat-pack furniture, BILLY, MALM, LACK, KALLAX, kitchens
  • Best for: affordable, well-designed furniture for first homes

"To create a better everyday life for the many people."

— The IKEA vision, IKEA (ikea.com)

4. Nilkamal

Nilkamal is the plastic chair in almost every Indian home, school and office. The company was founded in Mumbai in 1981 by brothers Vamanrai and Sharad Parekh, who started by making plastic household items in a rented unit in Powai. After seeing rows of plastic chairs at an exhibition in Germany in the late 1980s, they ordered a chair mould and began making moulded furniture in India.

Today Nilkamal is described as the world's largest manufacturer of moulded furniture. The range runs from the familiar Novella, Captain and Heritage plastic chairs to dining tables, shoe racks, storage and office furniture, plus its @Home retail chain, launched in 2005, for wooden home furniture. Choose Nilkamal when you want light, stackable, washable furniture at an everyday price — and a chair you can buy in almost any Indian town.

  • Brand owner: Nilkamal Limited
  • Founded: 1981, Mumbai
  • Known for: moulded plastic chairs, tables and storage; @Home stores
  • Best for: everyday plastic furniture for home, office and outdoors

Check Nilkamal NS08 chairs on Amazon

Check the Nilkamal Heritage chair on Amazon

5. Durian

Durian began in Mumbai in 1981, when Sajjan Dokania started trading in plywood, and moved into furniture in 1985. The company still makes its own plywood, laminates, veneers and doors, which is why its furniture is built on materials it controls from the factory floor up. Its first modular furniture facility opened in Palghar, Maharashtra, in 2006.

The range covers sofas and sofa sets, recliners, beds, dining tables, centre tables, desks and office chairs, sold through its own stores in more than thirty Indian cities and online. Durian suits shoppers who want a solid, mid-market Indian brand — furniture made in India, with a showroom nearby to sit on it first.

  • Brand owner: Durian Industries Ltd.
  • Founded: 1981, Mumbai; furniture since 1985
  • Known for: sofas, beds, dining sets, office furniture, plywood and laminates
  • Best for: sturdy, mid-market Indian-made home and office furniture

6. WoodenStreet

WoodenStreet is India's first online custom-furniture store. It was launched in June 2015 in Jaipur by Lokendra Singh Ranawat with co-founders Virendra Ranawat, Dinesh Pratap Singh and Vikas Baheti, who saw that Indian shoppers could not get furniture made to their own size and finish. The first experience store opened in Bengaluru soon after, and the brand now runs more than a hundred stores across India.

The pitch is customisation: solid-wood furniture — mostly sheesham, teak and white ash — made to order in Rajasthan, from beds and wardrobes to dining sets and study tables, with a choice of finishes and sizes. WoodenStreet suits shoppers who want real wood, a design of their own, and a price below the luxury boutiques.

  • Brand owner: The Woodenstreet Furnitures Pvt. Ltd.
  • Launched: June 2015, Jaipur
  • Known for: custom solid-wood furniture, beds, dining sets, wardrobes
  • Best for: made-to-order wooden furniture in your own finish

7. Evok

Evok is the home-interiors brand of Hindware, the sanitaryware group. It was launched in 2008 by Hindware Home Retail, a subsidiary of HSIL (now Hindware Home Innovation), which set out to build large-format home destination stores. The first Evok stores opened in the National Capital Region, and the brand has since spread to other Indian cities.

An Evok store is a one-stop home shop: furniture, furnishings, modular kitchens and wardrobes, bath products, flooring, lighting and lifestyle accessories, sourced from India and abroad. Evok suits shoppers who are furnishing a new home and want the furniture, the kitchen and the lighting decided in a single visit.

  • Brand owner: Hindware Home Retail (HSIL / Hindware Home Innovation)
  • Launched: 2008, National Capital Region
  • Known for: furniture, furnishings, modular kitchens and wardrobes
  • Best for: furnishing a new home in one destination store

8. Stanley

Stanley is India's home-grown luxury furniture brand, and it began with car seats. Promoter Sunil Suresh started in Bengaluru in 1996, reupholstering car seats in leather, and formed the partnership firm Stanley Seating on 1 February 2007. The first Stanley retail store opened in Bengaluru in 2011, and the company listed on the stock exchanges in June 2024.

The range is super-premium and luxury: leather sofas in many configurations, beds, wardrobes and kitchen cabinets, made in its own Bengaluru factories and sold through its Stanley Level Next, Stanley Boutique and Sofas & More stores. Stanley suits buyers who want genuine leather, custom sizes and a luxury showroom experience — and are willing to pay for it.

  • Brand owner: Stanley Lifestyles Ltd.
  • Founded: 2007, Bengaluru; first store 2011
  • Known for: luxury leather sofas, beds, wardrobes, kitchens
  • Best for: premium leather furniture and custom luxury interiors

9. Featherlite

Featherlite is the office-furniture name behind thousands of Indian workplaces. It was founded in Bengaluru in 1965 by Gopal Ramnarayan, who began making lightweight aluminium garden furniture — the "feather-light" idea behind the name. The company moved into office furniture in 1975, and into modular furniture in the 1980s, as India's corporate offices began to grow.

Today Featherlite makes office chairs, workstations, executive tables, partitions, education and healthcare furniture from its Bengaluru plants, and sells through direct and franchise offices across India. Its credo is "Work Better, Live Better". Featherlite suits anyone furnishing an office, a study or a workspace — and anyone who wants a chair built for eight hours a day, not eight minutes.

  • Brand owner: Featherlite Group
  • Founded: 1965, Bengaluru
  • Known for: office chairs, workstations, modular office furniture
  • Best for: home offices and workplaces that need ergonomic seating

10. HomeTown

HomeTown is the home-furnishing chain with the friendliest promise in this guide: "The Art of Better Living". It was launched by Future Retail in April 2007, with its first store in Noida, as a large-format destination for furniture and home decor. The brand now sells online and through stores, covering the whole house from the living room to the kitchen.

The range is broad and mid-market: sofas and beds, dining sets and wardrobes, mattresses, furnishings, decor and lighting, with regular value offers. HomeTown suits families furnishing a new flat on a budget — a single store where the sofa, the bed, the curtains and the lamps can all be chosen together.

  • Brand owner: HomeTown (launched by Future Retail)
  • Launched: April 2007; first store Noida
  • Known for: sofas, beds, dining sets, furnishings and home decor
  • Best for: value furniture and decor for a whole family home

11. Supreme Furniture

Supreme Furniture is the furniture arm of Supreme Industries, one of India's oldest plastics companies. Supreme Industries was incorporated in Mumbai on 17 February 1942, and the Taparia family took control in August 1966, making plastics processing the company's core business. Moulded furniture manufacturing began at its Noida unit in 1990–91.

The furniture range is the plastic classic: moulded chairs, tables, stools and storage that are light, stackable and weather-proof, sold across India through a vast dealer network. Supreme suits the practical buyer — a chair for the balcony, a table for the canteen, seating for a classroom or a wedding hall — where durability and price matter more than design.

  • Brand owner: Supreme Industries Ltd.
  • Founded: 1942, Mumbai; moulded furniture since 1990–91
  • Known for: moulded plastic chairs, tables and storage
  • Best for: durable, low-cost seating for home, school and events

12. Royaloak

Royaloak is the fastest-growing value retailer in this guide. It was founded in Bengaluru in 2010 by brothers Vijai and Mathan Subramaniam, starting with a single 200 sq ft store. From there it grew through franchise stores into more than 200 stores across 110-plus Indian cities, with an online store alongside.

The pitch is international-style furniture at Indian prices: sofas and recliners, beds, dining sets, wardrobes and decor, with a strong presence in smaller cities where the big online brands have few stores. Royaloak suits shoppers outside the metros who want a showroom they can walk into, and a full home's worth of furniture under one roof.

  • Brand owner: Royaloak Incorporation Pvt. Ltd.
  • Founded: 2010, Bengaluru
  • Known for: sofas, recliners, beds, dining sets, wardrobes
  • Best for: value furniture with a store in your city

13. Furlenco

Furlenco is the odd one out in this guide, and that is its charm: it does not sell furniture, it rents it. It was founded in Bengaluru in 2012 by Ajith Mohan Karimpana, a former Goldman Sachs banker, who started it as RentUrDuniya and later rebranded it as Furlenco. In 2023, Sheela Foam — the Sleepwell mattress maker — bought a 35% stake in the company.

The model is a monthly subscription: Furlenco designs its own furniture, delivers it, installs it and takes it away when you move, with free relocation in its cities. It suits renters, students and young professionals who move often — a furnished home without the cost of buying, and without the trouble of selling when the lease ends.

  • Brand owner: Kieraya Furnishing Solutions (Furlenco); Sheela Foam holds a 35% stake
  • Founded: 2012, Bengaluru
  • Known for: furniture rental and subscription, own-designed ranges
  • Best for: rented homes, short stays and frequent movers

14. Bent Chair

Bent Chair is the design-led brand for shoppers who find ordinary furniture boring. It was started in Delhi in August 2016 by Natasha Jain with her father Neeraj Jain, after Natasha could not find furniture she liked for her own new home. The brand designs and makes its own products, with manufacturing in Ambala, and sells online and through studios and franchise stores.

The style is bold and quirky: statement chairs, colourful cabinets, unusual lamps and wall art, often made with Indian artisans and craftspeople, under the Bent Chair and N atelier labels. Bent Chair suits buyers who want one piece that starts a conversation — a chair, a bar cabinet or a mirror that no neighbour will have.

  • Brand owner: Bent Chair
  • Started: August 2016, Delhi
  • Known for: bold, quirky designer furniture, decor and lighting
  • Best for: statement pieces and design-led homes

15. Furniturewalla

Furniturewalla is the luxury name at the end of this guide. It was founded in Mumbai in 1999 by Farhan Furniturewalla, and describes itself as a premium brand of luxury furniture, lighting, art and home decor. It retails from four signature stores in Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

The range is contemporary luxury: designer sofas and beds, dining tables, lighting and art, chosen from international trends and made for large, well-appointed homes. Furniturewalla suits buyers furnishing a premium home who want a curated, boutique experience — and a store where the furniture, the lighting and the art are chosen together.

  • Brand owner: Furniturewalla (FW)
  • Founded: 1999, Mumbai
  • Known for: luxury furniture, lighting, art and home decor
  • Best for: premium, design-led homes and boutique shopping

How to Choose a Furniture Brand

Start with the room, not the brand. A bedroom needs a bed and a wardrobe first; a living room needs a sofa that fits the wall; a study needs a chair you can sit in for hours. List the pieces you actually need, measure the room and the doorways, and only then shortlist brands that make those pieces well.

Match the material to the use. Solid wood suits furniture that stays put for years; flat-pack suits rented flats and first homes; moulded plastic suits balconies, classrooms and outdoor use; leather suits a living room that is used daily and cleaned often. Ask what the frame is made of — not just what it looks like.

Sit on it before you buy it. A sofa that looks good in a photograph can feel wrong in person, and a chair's comfort cannot be judged from a screen. Visit a store for the big pieces — a bed, a sofa, an office chair — and buy the small pieces online once you trust the brand.

Check delivery, assembly and warranty in writing. Large furniture needs delivery to the room, assembly, and packaging removal. Check who does it, what it costs, and how long the warranty lasts — Godrej Interio and Nilkamal, for example, state a one-year warranty on many products. A cheap price with no assembly is rarely cheap once you pay a carpenter.

Think about moving day. If you rent, or expect to move within a few years, flat-pack furniture and rental services such as Furlenco are worth more than heavy solid wood. Buy the permanent pieces — a good bed, a good chair — and rent or buy light for the rest.

FAQs

Which is the best furniture brand in India?

There is no single answer — it depends on your home, budget and taste. Godrej Interio is the safest all-rounder; IKEA leads on affordable design; Urban Ladder and WoodenStreet suit online and custom buying; Nilkamal and Supreme lead on everyday plastic furniture; and Stanley and Furniturewalla lead on luxury. This guide is an editorial selection to help you choose, not an official ranking.

Which brand is best for a first home on a budget?

IKEA, Urban Ladder and Royaloak are the natural starting points: flat-pack and value ranges keep costs down, and all three sell online with delivery. If you are renting, consider Furlenco — a monthly subscription furnishes the home without the cost of buying, and the furniture goes back when you move.

Which brands make solid-wood furniture?

WoodenStreet is the clearest choice: it specialises in custom solid-wood furniture in sheesham and teak. Godrej Interio, Durian and Royaloak also sell wooden beds, wardrobes and dining sets, though their ranges mix solid wood with engineered wood — check the product description for the exact material.

Which brands are best for office furniture?

Featherlite is the specialist, with office chairs, workstations and executive tables built for long working days. Godrej Interio is the other strong choice, with its Curv, Vurv and Prime ergonomic chairs and full office ranges. Both also sell through Amazon India, so you can compare current prices there.

Is it better to buy furniture online or in a store?

Buy small, standard pieces online — chairs, tables, storage — where the product is easy to judge. Visit a store for the big pieces: a sofa, a bed or a dining set. Sit on the sofa, lie on the bed, open the wardrobe doors. Most brands in this guide sell both ways, so you can research online and confirm in a store.

Why does this guide not list prices?

Furniture prices vary by city, size, finish, retailer and season, and change too often for a guide to stay accurate. We link to Amazon India for the brands sold there so you can see the current price before buying.

Conclusion

India's furniture market rewards both loyalty and curiosity. Keep a dependable everyday brand in mind for the pieces you use daily, back the Indian makers — Godrej Interio, Nilkamal, Durian, WoodenStreet and Featherlite — when you want furniture made in India, and leave room for the Swedish, luxury and rental ideas when the occasion calls for them. Whichever brand you choose, measure the room, sit on the sofa, and check the warranty before you pay.

Research note: Brand backgrounds in this guide were checked against the brands' official websites, company histories and reputable profiles in November 2026. Ranges and product names are as the brands themselves describe them; availability varies by city. If you spot an error, please contact VisitBest so we can correct it.

title.rendered: Top 18 Event Management Companies in Bangalore (2026)

content.rendered:
Quick answer first, then the detailed list — 18 event management companies with a verified Bangalore presence, for weddings, corporate events, conferences, concerts and exhibitions, each with its Bangalore base or office and its specialisation, and what to check before you book. Where a company publishes its official logo, we show it; the rest are described, never illustrated with a substitute mark.

Bangalore runs two event economies at once. Around Whitefield, Electronic City and the Outer Ring Road it is corporate India — product launches, developer conferences, dealer meets and some of the country's busiest tech-campus celebrations, fed by the IT corridor and the city's startup scene. Across the rest of the city it is celebration India — weddings at palace hotels and resort lawns towards Devanahalli and Nandi Hills, sangeets and receptions in Indiranagar and Koramangala, and large-format concerts and festivals at BIEC and Palace Grounds. The best event management companies in Bangalore usually specialise in one of these worlds, and this list tells you which is which.

Every company below has a real Bangalore presence — a headquarters, a genuine office or substantial operations in the city — verified against its official website in November 2026. Experience figures are the companies' own published statements, attributed as such; we have not invented fees, phone numbers, ratings or review counts. Prices in this industry are quoted per event after a scope discussion, so any company that gives you a firm rate without seeing your brief should be treated with caution.

Quick Answer: Which Bangalore Event Company Should You Pick?

For large-scale sports, music and concert properties, start with DNA Entertainment Networks or Phase 1 Events and Experiences, both headquartered in Bangalore. For national corporate and experiential programmes that include Bangalore, start with Percept Limited, Wizcraft, Tamarind Global or Laqshya Live Experiences. For corporate conferences, summits and family days, look at Zeal Integrated, White Massif, V Productions and Showmaker. For weddings, the shortlist splits by style: Tamarind Global and Page3 Events for luxury and large-format celebrations, The Tales of Tradition and Kraftstar Management for design-led and destination weddings. For offsites, MICE and team building, use Showmaker, Erigo Events, Eventz Unlimited or DreamCraft Events and Entertainment. For product launches and brand activations, use Wizcraft, DNA Entertainment Networks, Erigo Events or Page3 Events.

How to Choose an Event Management Company in Bangalore

Bangalore has hundreds of organisers, and the difference between a smooth event and a stressful one is usually paperwork, not taste. Before you pay any advance:

  • Get the scope in writing. An itemised quote that separates venue, catering, décor, sound, lighting, artists, photography and management fee. Vague lump sums are where budgets leak.
  • Ask what is produced in-house. Firms with their own staging, fabrication, AV and décor teams (several on this list have them) recover faster when something changes on the day.
  • Check references for a similar event. A company brilliant at sangeets may be new to 2,000-delegate conferences. Ask for two clients with events like yours and actually call them.
  • Confirm permissions and licences. Concerts, outdoor events and liquor service in Bangalore need police, excise and venue permissions; your contract should name who obtains them.
  • Pin the cancellation and postponement terms. Weather, artist dropout and venue issues happen. The refund ladder and date-shift policy belong in the agreement, not in a WhatsApp chat.
  • Fix the payment schedule. Tie payments to milestones (booking, production start, event day, closure) and list what is excluded — GST, venue charges, generator fuel and overtime are the usual surprises.
  • Name the event-day commander. One person with authority to spend and decide on the day, with a phone number that is answered.
  • Allow for Bangalore traffic. Load-in and artist movement across the Outer Ring Road and Whitefield corridor can take far longer than the map suggests — build the buffer into the run sheet, not into the show.

Treat DNA as the shortlist-topper for a large-format live event — a stadium property, a music festival or a marquee corporate show — rather than for a single family function.
